entry.title: iVolve Series | Part D : Beyond Go-Live
entry.content:
Note: This blog is a continuation of The iVolve Series | Your Integration Estate Is Holding You Back. Well, It Doesn’t Have To. Read iVolve Series | Part C: Automate Everything before continuing.

Go-live is not the end of an integration modernisation programme. It is the beginning of a new operating model. For many organisations, the transition from legacy middleware to SAP Integration Suite on BTP represents the first time their integration landscape has been managed with cloud-native DevOps practices i.e. continuous deployment, automated governance, proactive monitoring, and genuine high availability.

The challenge is that SAP Integration Suite, while a powerful platform, does not come with enterprise-grade DevOps tooling out of the box. Organisations that invest in a migration without investing in the operational layer often find themselves replicating the operational debt of the legacy landscape on a newer platform.

Tarento's OpEase Suite was built to close this gap. This blog examines the four key components and how they work together to deliver a resilient, well-governed, AI-enhanced integration operations environment.

 

OneFailover : Near-Zero Downtime for Critical Landscapes

For large integration landscapes handling business-critical transactions, planned and unplanned downtime is not just an IT inconvenience; it is a business risk with measurable financial impact. SAP Integration Suite maintenance windows, regional incidents, or platform upgrades can require traffic to be rerouted to a standby environment. Without tooling, this is a manual, error-prone process that takes hours and relies on precise coordination across multiple teams.

OneFailover provides an operational layer that standardises and automates this process entirely.

How OneFailover Works

OneFailover continuously maintains a failover tenant or runtime in a 'ready state' fully synchronised with the primary environment, tested, and prepared for immediate cutover. The core capabilities span several dimensions:

  • Sync & Orchestration: Full-scope synchronisation of iFlows, Message Mappings, Value Mappings, and Scripts across tenants, with dependency-aware ordering and group/sub-group priorities
  • Failover Control: Group-based methodology with deployment prioritisation and manual listener cutover, using OneFailover Profiles to map primary-to-failover configurations
  • Backup & Restore: GitHub-based, artefact-level versioning with selective restore capability and overwrite guardrails
  • Runtime Awareness: Edge Cell and multi-runtime/tenant awareness, with a persistence layer to inventory iFlows and tenant metadata
  • Observability: Operational Status and Monitoring dashboards, Readiness scores, activity and execution logs, and throughput optimisations
  • Security: User Credentials, Global Variables, Number Ranges, and Access Policies included in sync and backup, with secret-safe metadata handling

     

OneFailover integrates with enterprise routing patterns including Azure Traffic Manager, internal DNS solutions like F5 or Citrix NetScaler, and GitHub for version control, fitting naturally into existing enterprise infrastructure.

 

When to Use OneFailover

OneFailover is relevant across four operational scenarios: planned maintenance windows where manual coordination effort needs to be eliminated; regional resiliency programmes where a failover posture for critical interfaces must be maintained continuously; peak events where failover needs to be pre-staged for traffic surges; and compliance and audit requirements where evidence of DR readiness and traceable execution history is needed.

 

iFlow AI Advisory App : Design Intelligence for Dev Ease

The iFlow AI Advisory App addresses a challenge that emerges as integration teams start developing new flows and extending migrated ones on SAP Integration Suite: without deep platform expertise, developers default to familiar patterns from legacy platforms that are not optimal on BTP.

The iFlow AI Advisory App provides automated design recommendations, guiding integration teams to the most appropriate iFlow patterns for each use case. Rather than waiting for an architecture review to flag suboptimal designs, the advisory capability operates at development time, preventing technical debt from accumulating in the new landscape before it has even started.

This capability is particularly valuable for organisations that are extending their SAP Integration Suite footprint beyond the migrated interfaces into net-new integration development, ensuring that the same automation-first, pattern-led approach that characterised the migration carries through into ongoing development.

 

Transport Management & Governance Tool

Governance of the integration landscape, managing the lifecycle of iFlows from development through QA to production, is a critical operational capability that is easy to underestimate. Without structured transport management, teams resort to manual deployment procedures, version confusion, and the risk of deploying untested changes to production.

The iVolve Transport Management and Governance Tool provides the operational rigour that enterprise integration landscapes require:

  • Full transport management capabilities with controlled promotion from development through QA to production
  • Artefact comparison and version management -> compare versions before deployment to understand exactly what is changing
  • Easy access to adapter configuration details across the landscape
  • Externalised parameter management for environment-specific configurations

 

Enhanced Monitoring and AI-Powered Operations

SAP Integration Suite's native monitoring provides a solid baseline, but enterprise operations teams consistently find they need capabilities that go further particularly around error management, reporting, and proactive intelligence.

Enhanced Monitoring Tool

Built on SAP standards for seamless integration, the Enhanced Monitoring Tool provides full monitoring reports with downloadable error outputs for efficient debugging. Its restart functionality and searchable interface  by sender, receiver, message type, application ID, date, time, and statistical aggregates, enables operations teams to move from reactive firefighting to proactive management.

AI-Powered Alert Notifications

iVolve's AI-enhanced notification capability leverages SAP BTP's Integration Suite AI Adapter to enrich alert emails with GenAI-generated recommendations, giving operations teams not just the notification of a failure, but context-aware guidance on likely causes and resolution steps. This is the beginning of a shift from monitoring to intelligence-assisted operations.

Periodic Monitoring AI Agent

Looking ahead to the 2026 roadmap, Tarento is building out an autonomous Periodic Monitoring Agent that will automate routine manual monitoring activities using the iVolve AI platform, removing the operational overhead of scheduled checks and exception reviews from the integration operations team entirely.

 

The OpEase Suite as a Competitive Advantage

 Organisations that deploy the full OpEase Suite alongside their SAP Integration Suite migration achieve something qualitatively different from those that treat DevOps as an afterthought. They have a resilient, governed, intelligence-enhanced integration operations model from day one of go-live. Their operations teams are not firefighting  but are managing by exception, with tooling that surfaces the information they need and automates the responses they would otherwise need to execute manually.

 

 

Bringing It All Together: The Full iVolve Journey

Across this series, we have traced the complete arc of integration modernisation with iVolve; from the strategic imperative and business case, through automated discovery, migration and testing, to the operational excellence of the OpEase Suite. In the next and final blog of this series, we will deep dive into OneFailOver Application and how it helps enterprises architect and manage high-resiliency, and take control over the HA/Failover process in their organisations.

Across the series, the consistent thread has been automation: reducing the manual effort, the human error, and the programme risk that have historically made integration modernisation programmes difficult to justify and difficult to deliver.

Tarento’s iVolve programme is the product of deep SAP integration expertise, proprietary tooling built and refined over dozens of programmes, and a genuine commitment to delivering the ROI that customers calculate before they commit.

entry.title: iVolve Series | Part E : When Downtime Is Not an Option
entry.content:
Note: This blog is part of The iVolve Series | Your Integration Estate Is Holding You Back. Well, It Doesn’t Have To. Read the previous blog in this series, iVolve Series | Part D : Beyond Go-Live before continuing.

It is 11:47 PM. An online retailer’s Black Friday weekend promotion has just gone live. Orders are flooding in at three times the normal rate. Every order triggers a cascade of integration events; stock reservation, payment confirmation, warehouse dispatch, carrier booking, customer notification. All of this runs through SAP Integration Suite. And at 11:52 PM, comes an announcement of an emergency platform maintenance window. The primary tenant will be unavailable for the next 45 minutes.

For organisations without a failover strategy, this is a crisis. For organisations running OneFailover, it is a non-event. Traffic is rerouted to the failover tenant in seconds. The integration landscape keeps running. And the end customers never notice. Seamless as seamless can be!

This blog examines why integration resilience is a board-level concern for any enterprise that relies on SAP Integration Suite for real-time business operations and how Tarento’s OneFailover application transforms a complex, manual, high-risk process into a repeatable, automated, and auditable programme capability.

 

The Integration Layer Is the Business

For a previous generation of enterprises, integration middleware was infrastructure; important, but not business-critical in the way that customer-facing systems were. That distinction has collapsed. For any organisation that has consolidated its integration estate onto SAP Integration Suite, the platform is now the nervous system of real-time business operations.

Consider the industries where this is most acute. A large e-commerce retailer processes tens of thousands of orders per hour during peak periods; every order is an integration event. A global manufacturer runs real-time production planning and supplier collaboration through integration flows; a 30-minute outage ripples into production delays, penalty clauses, and customer escalations. A financial services firm processes payment instructions and regulatory reporting through integration; downtime is a compliance exposure, not just an operational inconvenience. A healthcare provider coordinates patient data flows, bed management, and pharmacy dispensing through its integration platform; unavailability can directly affect patient outcomes.

For all of these organisations, the question of what happens when SAP Integration Suite is unavailable - whether for a planned maintenance window, a regional incident, or a capacity event is not a theoretical IT risk. It is a live business continuity question that demands a credible, tested answer.

 

The Downtime Problem Is More Complex Than It Looks

SAP Integration Suite is a managed cloud service. This brings enormous benefits - Continuous updates, elastic scaling, no infrastructure management overhead. But it also means that maintenance is scheduled by SAP, not by the enterprise. Planned maintenance windows are notified in advance but are not negotiable. And unplanned incidents, while rare on a well-operated cloud platform, cannot be eliminated entirely.

The naïve response is to simply provision a second tenant and manually copy everything across when needed. In practice, this approach fails in three ways.

First, the synchronisation problem: a large integration landscape may contain hundreds of iFlows, message mappings, value mappings, scripts, security artefacts, and configuration parameters. Keeping a secondary tenant in sync with all of these manually is a significant ongoing operational burden, one that is frequently deprioritised until it is too late.

Second, the execution problem: when an incident occurs or a maintenance window opens, switching traffic to a secondary tenant requires precise, sequenced steps across multiple systems - DNS or traffic manager changes, iFlow activation, listener cutover, and verification. Doing this under pressure, manually, from a runbook, at 2 AM, creates unacceptable risk of human error.

Third, the governance problem: many regulated industries require documented, auditable evidence of disaster recovery capability. A manual failover process that lives in a shared document and has never been tested in a controlled way does not satisfy this requirement.

 

The Three Failure Modes of Manual Failover

Synchronisation drift means the failover tenant is never truly ready. Execution risk means the switchover itself is the most dangerous moment. Governance gaps mean the organisation cannot demonstrate readiness to auditors or regulators. OneFailover addresses all three simultaneously.

 

 

Introducing OneFailover: An Operational Layer for Integration Resilience

OneFailover is Tarento’s purpose-built application for SAP Integration Suite tenant resilience — available on the SAP Store and used by enterprises running large, mission-critical integration landscapes. It was formerly known as Unified Failover Management and has evolved into a comprehensive operational platform that addresses every dimension of the failover challenge: continuous synchronisation, controlled cutover, backup and recovery, observability, and governance.

The core design principle is that failover should never be an emergency response. It should be a routine, well-rehearsed capability that an operations team can invoke with confidence, whether for a scheduled maintenance window, a regional resiliency exercise, or an actual incident. OneFailover is built around that principle from the ground up.

 

The Six Pillars of OneFailover

 Pillar 1: Continuous Sync and Orchestration

OneFailover maintains a full-scope, continuously synchronised replica of the primary tenant across all artefact types: iFlows, Message Mappings, Value Mappings, and Scripts. Synchronisation is dependency-aware, artefacts that depend on each other are always moved together, in the correct sequence, preventing partial deployments that would cause failures. Group and sub-group priorities allow integration teams to define which business domains and interface clusters are synchronised first, ensuring the most critical processes are always in the highest state of readiness on the failover tenant. Single-side or both-side deployment options give teams flexibility in how they manage the synchronisation cadence.

Pillar 2: Failover Control and Cutover Execution

When the moment of cutover arrives, planned or unplanned, OneFailover provides deterministic, orchestrated execution. The group-based methodology ensures that interface clusters are activated on the failover tenant in the correct business-aware sequence: order management before warehouse execution, payment before fulfilment. OneFailover Profiles capture the complete primary-to-failover mapping configuration, including Git targets, so that the same cutover procedure can be repeated identically every time - in a drill, in a maintenance window, or in a genuine incident. An admin lock prevents simultaneous actions by multiple operators during a cutover, eliminating the risk of conflicting changes in a high-pressure situation. Manual listener cutover ensures that human confirmation is required at the point of traffic switching, maintaining control at the most consequential moment.

The cutover integrates with enterprise routing infrastructure. For inbound traffic switching, OneFailover works with Azure Traffic Manager in a priority-based setup, or with internal DNS solutions such as F5 or Citrix NetScaler, fitting into the network architecture that the enterprise already operates rather than requiring new infrastructure to be introduced.

Pillar 3: Backup, Restore and Version Control

OneFailover provides GitHub-based, artefact-level versioning for the integration landscape. Every iFlow, mapping, and configuration is versioned individually, enabling selective restore with overwrite guardrails that prevent accidental rollbacks. Failover configurations, the OneFailover Profiles, can be exported and imported, enabling them to be maintained, version-controlled, and shared across teams. This creates a complete audit trail of the integration landscape’s state over time, supporting change management, incident investigation, and regulatory compliance requirements.

Pillar 4: Multi-Runtime and Multi-Tenant Awareness

Large enterprise integration landscapes are not homogeneous. They typically span multiple SAP Integration Suite tenants, multiple runtimes including Cloud Foundry and Edge Integration Cells for sensitive on-premise data, and multiple business domains with different criticality levels and ownership. OneFailover is designed for this complexity. Its persistence layer maintains a complete inventory of iFlows and tenant metadata across the full landscape, providing a single point of control and visibility regardless of how many tenants and runtimes are in scope. Edge Cell awareness means that even hybrid landscapes  with interfaces running on-premise for data sovereignty or latency reasons, are fully included in the failover posture.

Pillar 5: Observability and Operational Dashboards

Knowing that a failover tenant exists is not the same as knowing that it is ready. OneFailover provides continuous Readiness Scores for each tenant and runtime, a quantified measure of how current the failover environment is relative to the primary, how recently it was tested, and whether any synchronisation gaps or configuration discrepancies exist. Operational Status and Monitoring dashboards give integration operations teams real-time visibility into the state of both primary and failover environments, with activity and execution logs that provide a complete record of every action taken. Throughput optimisations ensure that synchronisation activity does not create performance overhead on the primary tenant during business hours.

Pillar 6: Security, Compliance and Secret Safety

Integration landscapes contain sensitive security artefacts: User Credentials, Global Variables, Number Ranges, and Access Policies. OneFailover includes all of these in its synchronisation and backup scope, ensuring that the failover tenant is not just functionally complete but operationally ready to process real transactions. Security is maintained through SAP BTP Identity Authentication Service-powered authentication and strict secret-safe metadata handling: credentials and sensitive values are referenced by hash or reference only, never stored in plain text in version control. Strong guardrails prevent accidental exposure of production credentials during failover operations.

 

Why SAP’s Standard Capabilities Are Not Enough: The Case for OneFailover

A common assumption when enterprises first deploy SAP Integration Suite is that high availability and disaster recovery are simply included, that because SAP is a managed cloud service, the resilience problem is solved by default. This assumption is partially correct and significantly incomplete. SAP Integration Suite does provide genuine, well-engineered high availability within a single region through multi-availability zone redundancy.

For most routine operational scenarios, the above is sufficient. But for enterprises that require cross-regional disaster recovery, planned maintenance execution without service interruption, automated failover with deterministic cutover sequences, and the kind of audit-ready, governance-controlled resilience posture that regulated industries must demonstrate, SAP’s native capabilities leave substantial gaps that OneFailover is specifically engineered to fill.

The table below maps each dimension of enterprise integration resilience against what SAP provides natively and what OneFailover adds, making explicit where the standard platform ends and where OneFailover begins.

The pattern across every dimension in this table is consistent: SAP provides the foundation, and OneFailover provides the operational layer that transforms that foundation into a fully governed, automated, and enterprise-grade resilience posture. These are capabilities that matter most when a regional incident, a regulatory audit, or a peak trading event puts real pressure on the integration landscape. Treating them as optional is, in effect, a decision to accept that risk rather than manage it.

For integration teams making the case internally for OneFailover investment, this table is often the most effective starting point: it places SAP’s own standard offering alongside OneFailover’s capabilities, making the gap visible and the value proposition concrete across every dimension that leadership, operations, and compliance stakeholders care about.

 

Planning for the Four Scenarios That Matter

OneFailover’s capabilities map directly onto the four operational scenarios where integration resilience is genuinely tested:

Scenario 1: Planned Maintenance Windows

SAP notifies maintenance windows in advance, giving integration teams time to prepare. With OneFailover, preparation is straightforward: verify the Readiness Score, run a pre-cutover sync to ensure the failover tenant reflects all recent changes, and execute the controlled cutover through the OneFailover portal. The maintenance window passes with no business disruption. When the primary tenant is restored, failback follows the same orchestrated process in reverse. What would otherwise require a team of engineers working through a complex runbook becomes a two-person operation managed through an intuitive interface.

Scenario 2: Regional Resiliency and Unplanned Incidents

For organisations with a global integration landscape, regional incidents like a cloud availability zone event, a network disruption, a regional regulatory action etc may require rerouting integration traffic to a different data centre or availability zone. The risk calculus has also shifted. Recent geopolitical conflicts most notably the US/Israel and Iran confrontation have seen data centres targeted as part of military operations, causing prolonged regional outages that no amount of within-region redundancy could mitigate. Cloud infrastructure is not insulated from the consequences of armed conflict, and organisations with dependencies in or routing through affected regions are finding that out in real time. Regional resilience is no longer a contingency for rare technical failures it is a standing operational requirement. 

OneFailover’s multi-tenant and multi-runtime awareness, combined with its integration with Azure Traffic Manager and enterprise DNS infrastructure, makes regional rerouting a controlled operation rather than a crisis response. The failover tenant in a secondary region is continuously maintained in a ready state so that when rerouting is needed, whether triggered by a scheduled maintenance window or an unplanned regional event, the tenant is already current and the cutover can be executed without scrambling to synchronise artefacts under pressure.

Scenario 3: Peak Traffic Events

For e-commerce retailers, peak trading periods i.e. Black Friday, Cyber Monday, end-of-season sales etc represent the highest-value and highest-risk windows of the year. An integration outage during a 48-hour peak event can represent millions in lost revenue and lasting reputational damage. OneFailover provides the assurance that integration teams need to approach peak periods with confidence: a fully synchronised, tested, and ready failover tenant that can absorb traffic within seconds if the primary environment comes under strain or experiences an incident. The Readiness Score dashboard gives leadership a quantified, real-time view of DR preparedness in the days and hours before a peak event goes live.

Scenario 4: Compliance, Audit and DR Certification

Regulated industries; financial services, healthcare, utilities, public sector are increasingly required to demonstrate integration resilience as part of broader IT operational resilience or business continuity frameworks. The EU’s Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA), for example, requires financial entities to test their ICT continuity measures, maintain documented recovery procedures, and demonstrate that critical third-party dependencies, including cloud platforms are covered by their resilience programmes.

OneFailover’s activity logs, execution records, Readiness Scores, and repeatable playbooks provide exactly the evidence base that internal audit, external auditors, and regulators need to see: documented DR capability, tested regularly, with traceable execution history.

 

What Enterprises Gain: The Business Value Equation

 OneFailover delivers value across four dimensions that map directly to business outcomes rather than IT metrics:

  • Lower operational risk: integration outages during maintenance windows, peak events, or incidents are eliminated as a source of business disruption. The risk is not mitigated but is engineered out of the operating model
  • Faster, repeatable failover: what previously took hours of manual coordination is reduced to minutes of portal-guided execution. The same process runs identically every time, removing the dependency on tribal knowledge and individual expertise
  • Improved governance: every action is logged, every artefact is versioned, and every failover execution is traceable. The integration landscape becomes auditable in a way it never was with legacy middleware or manual processes
  • Higher confidence: integration teams, operations leadership, and the business can approach maintenance windows and peak events knowing that the failover posture is quantified, tested, and ready

 

 The 2026 Roadmap: Making OneFailover Even Smarter

Tarento’s 2026 roadmap for OneFailover extends the platform into several high-value adjacent areas. API Management integration will bring API policies and configurations into the sync and failover scope, ensuring that API-fronted integrations maintain consistent behaviour across primary and failover environments. A Centralised Key Vault integration will further strengthen the security model for credential and secret management across tenants. Advanced Proactive Alerting will shift OneFailover from a reactive tool into a predictive one, notifying operations teams of synchronisation drift or readiness degradation before it becomes a risk. Trading Partner Management capabilities will extend the failover posture to cover B2B integration configurations, ensuring that EDI and partner-facing integrations are included in the resilience framework alongside internal A2A flows.

 

Integration Resilience as a Programme Capability, Not an Afterthought

The organisations that get the most from SAP Integration Suite are those that treat it as a strategic platform, not just infrastructure. That means investing not only in migration quality and development standards, but in the operational model that keeps the platform running at the level of reliability the business requires.

For any enterprise where integration is the backbone of real-time business operations, whether in retail, manufacturing, financial services, healthcare, or logistics - OneFailover is not an optional enhancement to a well-functioning SAP Integration Suite deployment. It is the mechanism that makes a well-functioning deployment genuinely enterprise-ready: predictable, resilient, governed, and prepared for the scenarios that matter most.

The scenario at the start of this blog; an e-retailer navigating a Friday night urgent maintenance window at peak trading, illustrates what is at stake. With OneFailover, the answer to that scenario is simple: the integration landscape keeps running. The customers keep doing what they do. The business keeps moving. And when the primary tenant comes back online, failback runs just as cleanly as failover did.

Additional resource

Some times for partner based value mapping, we mainted the general data inside the transactions of an agreement, which can help during the dynamic field data mapping. to pick these values from agreement below code can be utilized. This code get the value from one of the header "ACTUAL_PARTNER_ID" which can be use to lookup inside the partnerDirectory data. All the general data we maintain under Activity paramters (agreement transaction) are stored under the "Binary parameter" with the ID "SAP_TPM_CustomActivityParams" in the form of JSon.

import com.sap.it.api.pd.PartnerDirectoryService;
import com.sap.it.api.ITApiFactory;
import com.sap.gateway.ip.core.customdev.util.Message;
import groovy.json.*;
import com.sap.it.api.pd.BinaryData;

def Message processData(Message message) {

    def pdService = ITApiFactory.getApi(PartnerDirectoryService.class, null)
    if (pdService == null) throw new Exception("Partner Directory Service not available")
    def partnerID = message.getHeaders().get("ACTUAL_PARTNER_ID");

    if (partnerID != null) {
        // dynamic parameters for custom activity
		def customActivityParams = pdService.getParameter("SAP_TPM_CustomActivityParams", partnerID, BinaryData.class);
		if (customActivityParams != null){
			def customActivityParamsStr = new String(customActivityParams.getData());
			def customActivityParamsJson = new JsonSlurper().parseText(customActivityParamsStr);
			customActivityParamsJson.each{
				paramKey, paramValue -> message.setProperty(paramKey, paramValue);
			}
		}
    }
    return message
}

Apart from these sometime complex value map can be maintained under Manager Partner Directory (under Manage Stores) which generally can be without partner specific but may be based on the Counrty, plant etc. This can be access with below code.

import com.sap.it.api.pd.PartnerDirectoryService
import com.sap.it.api.ITApiFactory
import com.sap.gateway.ip.core.customdev.util.Message

def Message processData(Message message) {
	
    // 1. Initialize Partner Directory Service
    def pdService = ITApiFactory.getApi(PartnerDirectoryService.class, null)
    if (pdService == null) throw new Exception("Partner Directory Service not available")

    // 2. Handle First PID (Suffix logic)
    // Assuming input PID comes from a header or property named 'Input_PID'
    String inputPid = message.getHeaders().get("PD_APID") ?: message.getProperties().get("PD_APID")
    
	if (inputPid) {
        String pid1 = inputPid + "_PD"
        String val1 = pdService.getParameter("SNDPRN", pid1, String.class)
		String val2 = pdService.getParameter("SNDPRT", pid1, String.class)
        message.setProperty("Partner_SNDPRN", val1 ?: "") // Empty if null
		message.setProperty("Partner_SNDPRT", val2 ?: "") // Empty if null
    }

    // 3. Handle Second PID (EDI_DC40_QA)
    String pid2 = message.getHeaders().get("SAP_ID") ?: message.getProperties().get("SAP_ID")
    
	// These can be changed based on the requirement and ID's which maintained uder Partner Directory
	def paramList = ["SNDPOR", "RCVPOR", "RCVPRT", "RCVPRN"]

    paramList.each { paramId ->
        String value = pdService.getParameter(paramId, pid2, String.class)
        // Store in property named 'Partner_SNDPRT', 'Partner_SNDPOR', etc.
        message.setProperty("Partner_" + paramId, value ?: "")
    }
    return message
}

entry.title: Introducing SAP Integration Suite, enhanced edition
entry.content:
Why Integration Suite Is Now the Most Strategic Investment for Your AI and Agentic AI Future 

Across every industry, companies are racing to adopt AI. However, the reality is that many organizations are experimenting with models, copilots, and prototypes, with just a smaller number managing to scale AI into real business operations. The reason for the wide gap between experimentation and enterprise level adoption is trust. Now, with SAP Integration Suite, enhanced edition, Agentic AI implementations can move from analyzing and experimenting to confidently acting. 

It’s a foundational shift in how businesses can safely, securely, and efficiently bring AI into the core of their operations. SAP Integration Suite, enhanced edition provides access to newly released AI features. These AI features include capabilities aimed at improving developer productivity and features that address operational efficiency.  

SAP Integration Suite, enhanced edition feature set 

Developer productivity features include:  

  • Text-to-Flow generation helps developers build integration flows using a natural language interface. 
  • Script Optimization enables developers to analyze, refactor, and optimize Groovy or JavaScript scripts used inside iFlows within SAP Integration Suite’s Cloud Integration component. 

Operations efficiency features include:  

  • API Anomaly Detection provides customers with AI-driven observability and monitoring by detecting unusual behavior in message processing and identifying integration issues early.  
  • API Traffic Prediction leverages AI-augmented design and governance capabilities within the API Management component, to assist developers and architects in discovering, designing, and optimizing APIs more intelligently. 

In addition to these powerful AI-orientated Integration features, SAP Integration Suite enhanced edition also provides customers with access to: 

  • The entire suite of integration capabilities: application-to-application integration, business-to-business integration, end-to-end API Management, edge integration capabilities, and hundreds of 3rd party connectors.  
  • Integration Suite, advanced event mesh for event driven architecture-based use cases. 
  • SAP Document AI converts unstructured data into structured data  
  • Alert Notification Service proactively alerts users about system events, anomalies, or errors across iFlows, APIs, and adapters. 
  • Transport Management Service moves integration artifacts and configurations across BTP subaccounts and landscapes without direct system access or manual export/import. 

Below, we break down why this release is so important and how it will help your organization accelerate into an AI-powered future. 

AI Needs Access. Agentic AI Needs Action. Integration Suite Enables Both. 

AI models are only as good as the data they can reach. Agentic AI goes a step further: it requires secure, governed pathways to take actions across systems—from creating a purchase order, to updating a vendor record, to executing a workflow. 

SAP Integration Suite provides: 

  • More Unified, governed connectivity to SAP and non-SAP systems 
  • Real-time event streams and APIs that support autonomous agent actions 
  • Standardized data models for consistent, reliable AI reasoning 
  • Workflow orchestration that ensures agents can complete end-to-end processes 

In other words: 
Integration Suite becomes the digital circulatory system that allows AI and Agentic AI to interact safely and intelligently with your valuable enterprise process and application data sources 

Why This Release Matters for Customers 

1. You Enable AI That Actually Works Across Your Enterprise Landscape 

Most companies run dozens—sometimes hundreds—of interconnected systems. Traditional AI pilots struggle because they operate in isolation. Integration Suite provides: 

  • Prebuilt connectors to your critical business systems 
  • Harmonized, real-time data flows 
  • A way to eliminate integration debt that slows down AI initiatives 

Your AI doesn’t stay stuck in a lab. It connects to your business. 

 2. You Unlock Agentic AI Capabilities Faster and More Safely 

Agentic AI can execute actions as directed, but enterprises require strict governance. Enhanced edition provides access controls, auditability, error handling, and regulates usage which allows companies to facilitate AI agents requests knowing that every action is secured, monitored, and fully reversible. 

 3. You Free Your Teams from Integration Bottlenecks 

Every AI use case requires connectivity. Before now, that meant long waits for custom integrations. 
With SAP Integration Suite: 

  • APIs, events, and integration flows become reusable assets 
  • Low-code tooling accelerates experimentation 
  • Citizen developers and integration teams get a shared workspace 

This means you can support AI use cases quickly when your business needs them. 

 4. You Prepare Your Landscape for a Hybrid, AI-Driven Future 

AI doesn’t just live in the cloud. Many mission-critical workloads remain on-premise or in private environments. Integration Suite ensures: 

  • AI can work across all your landscapes 
  • Legacy systems don’t become barriers to innovation 
  • You can adopt new AI capabilities without restructuring your architecture 

Supporting where your business runs today, maintaining ful compatibility with where AI is going tomorrow. 

 5. You Establish a Foundation for Scalable, Repeatable AI Value 

Each new integration flow, each API, each event—becomes part of a reusable catalog.  
Over time, your organization builds a growing library of AI-ready building blocks that accelerate every future use case. 

This creates compounding value, year after year. 

What This Means for Your Business Today 

With the enhancements in this release, SAP Integration Suite becomes more than a technical enabler — it becomes your Enterprise circulatory system And, most importantly It becomes the key accelerator that turns AI ideas into enterprise-grade, production-ready outcomes. 

What’s Next? 

This release is a major step in SAP’s broader vision of building an enterprise-ready AI ecosystem where: 

  • Data flows freely but securely 
  • Systems speak the same language 
  • AI operates with governance and trust 
  • Autonomous agents can navigate complex end-to-end processes 

We’re excited to see how you apply these new capabilities to unlock efficiency, fuel innovation, and reshape how work gets done.

entry.title: Integration Guardrails are more than Integration Patterns of the Composable Business
entry.content:
What are the Integration Patterns? Are those Guardrails? Or part of the overall Framework? Or just “simple” Building Blocks, either Architecture (ABBs) or Solution (SBBs)… It can be all, depending on the depth we want to go.

But things are changing.

Now we talk about Composable Business Architecture, again, continuing the story from the previous article[1][2][3]. We see Composable Business Architecture as a “style” built for Resilience, and more. Of course, Composable Business Architecture is not only about Resilience, but also about Agility, Speed, and about overall Leadership. It is by far more than just “technology”, but I will stick with the technology (at least a bit) in the article.

What is that what can enable us to be resilient, agile and have speed to react in the Intelligent Enterprise? We may need to adopt, to introduce now business process, replace some ABBs, or add some new and different SBBs. What is the glue connection all this?

It’s all about integrations… Integrations are seamlessly connecting everything with everyone. After all, aren’t we talking of Boundaryless Information Flow©?[4]?

Tides are shifting?

While in the “past” we could allow ourselves to be “framework” specific, things are changing now.

In previous articles (Part 1, Part 2, Part 3 and then Part 4 covering Omni-channel example) I was already talking about Integration Patterns, but focus was mostly around SAP Integration Solution Advisory Methodology (ISA-M)[5].

With building Composable Business, we are now distancing ourselves from the specific frameworks and methodologies, or even away from the specific products. The idea is “everything“ is just a ”replicable” box, and every box can be replaced with other box(s). We are looking at the pattens – only (high level) patterns. If and how those patterns are “manageable” with specific frameworks and/or methodologies, at least as specific Solution Guardrails – well, this is a different story, for some other article (perhaps?)…  

NEW Integration Patterns – simplified approach…

We should don’t try to overwhelm ourselves too much with terminology mess – what is Sync or Async. What is PULL vs. PUSH, what is batch vs. single record, is it Event or Data Streaming, is it Data Integration or Integration Service etc.

Look, we are always integrating Data, this integration can be triggered by Event (i.e. System or user-action) or schedule job, which will either PULL or PUSH some “message” sending or requesting some payload/dataset through API/EventAPI/message (i.e. message like AMQP wire protocol, which is not API), and this payload/dataset may contain some Notification, or one full Record, or Batch of many Records (which of course can be some delta or full “table”). Simple as that…

Things are not that complex?

Actually, they are, this is why AI is still not doing my job…

We will now observe only five distinct Integration Patterns and put all in one “simple” table:

But to connect with “old” terminology, lets re-explain a bit Data Integration Context:

  • Data Migration –one-time bulk data is PUSH/PULL from the Provider to the Consumer(s). Usually there is one Consumer).
  • Broadcast – data is PUSH from the Provider to the Consumer(s). Usually this is an Event based.
  • One-way synchronization – data is PUSH (or PULL in case of Sync Request-Reply GET call) from the Consumer to the Provider(s); where Consumer or the initiating System is notified of the synchronization status, either in Sync or Async mode.
  • Two-way synchronization – although one System is “formally” an owner (or Provider) of the Data Object, both (or many) Systems can initiate synchronization; data is PUSH (or PULL in case of Sync Request-Reply GET call) from one System to the other System(s); where each initiating System is notified of the synchronization status, either in Sync or Async mode. I.e. maintaining and synchronizing Vendor/Supplier between SAP MDG and SAP Ariba.
  • Data Correlation – both (or many) Systems are natural & independent Providers of the Data Object; intersection of data which is created naturally & independently is PUSH (or PULL in case of Sync Request-Reply GET call) from one System to the other System(s); where each initiating System is notified of the synchronization status. I.e. two Sales Agents creates the same Account in the different Systems – those Accounts will be synchronized, but if only one Sales Agent creates Account in one System – this Account will not be synchronized to the other System (will not be visible to the other Sales Agent);
  • Data Aggregation – there can be many Provider(s) but only one Consumer of the Data Object; data is PUSH (or PULL in case of Sync Request-Reply GET call) from the Provider(s) to the Consumer. i.e. pulling off the IoT readings; or ETL into DWH.

It is also wort mentioning some special Integration Scenarios:

  • Master Data Replication – by nature this is done in Async mode, but in majority of the cases we need to know the synchronizations status of the overall Data Object, in in some cases this is one single flow process. I.e. replication of the Business Partner Customer, related Business Partner Contact Persons, and its “link” via Business Partner Relationships.
  • EDI Messaging – this B2B Integration Scenario is specific Async integration style. I.e. for some EDI/AS2 messages Trade Partner will provide reply, but in some cases, this may not be mandatory nor expected.

What is visible here, none of the “old” or “special” patterns/scenarios in fact is clearly defining what exact Integration Patterns to apply. So, it can be misleading and prone to different interpretations. Here “new” Integration Patterns (and there are only five of them) is very specific and clear to understand – and of course, to implement.

First, it starts with Integration Principles…

Integration Principles are an equivalent to Architecture Principles – expressing our statement, and foundation rules we observe while designing the solutions.

There could be many, and it depends on form organization to organization. I.e. some examples could be

  1. Reuse existing Integration Services whenever possible – this implies we build for reusability, we do not create “multiple” instances for the same Integration Service for different Consumers. We try to build Integration Service once on the Provider and then reused by many Consumers.
  2. Consumer driven integration not only API driven – while this may sound a bit controversial, with this concept we will fully enforce layered API approach: System API, Business API and Experience API.
    Provider(s) provide System APIs/EventAPIs, but those might not meet holistic needs for cross-platform “reuse”.
    Therefore, gateways and middleware will provide Business APIs/EventAPIs, to meet most of the cross-platform “reuse”.
    Finally, individual Consumers may in fact still need to build on top it (i.e. combining several BusinessAPIs/EventAPIs), its own Experience APIs/EventAPIs, to meet the specific “customer experience” needs.
  3. Governance always – build something we can understand (i.e. Documentation), we can measure (i.e. Testing and Performance Testing) and we can manage (i.e. Monitoring and Observability implemented).
  4. Decoupled/Loosely-coupled integrations – enabling core components of the Composable Business Architecture – being able to sustain disruptive changes in the Business, Application and Technology domain, and continue "normal" operations (or more). This requires specific style of integrations – connecting Business Processes, Application Systems and Technology IT Components through decoupled patterns or connecting them loosely
  5. Standard APIs first – we avoid building custom integrations as the Provider, but try to use standard APIs as much as possible. We try to “adjusting” for various Consumers by “compensating/complementing in Business APIs, or mostly in Experience APIs layer.
  6. etc.

These are only few examples, and there could be more. Each organization will set its own “strong” statements – but let’s not overdo – let’s keep it within range of 3-5 main principles, which are clear and implementable.

Then, Integration Patterns

While we may identify some specific patterns, specific for our organization, I will limit the list here on these five:

  • Sync Request-Reply
  • Async Request-Reply
  • PubSub
  • E(T)L
  • DB Data Replication

Sync Request-Reply pattern

Figure 1. Sync Request-Reply

When to use

  • Real-time needed
  • Low or medium volumes
  • (Loosely-)coupled

Rules:

  • Use API-M as an entry point
  • Use middleware (CPI) for mapping/orchestration

Anti-patterns:

  • Point-to-point integration from client to backend
  • Long-running sync calls – if so, use Async

Explained:

  • Sync Request-Reply is a single thread, so only one operation will run at a time. System sending Request will wait for that Request to be answered by the other System (=Response), before continuing with other operations. Usually, this is used to encapsulate the transaction(s).
  • Requestor (System sending Request Message) will wait for the response from the Responder (System sending Response Message).

Examples of use:

  • SAP Commerce Cloud and other Order taking channels in the Omni-channel landscape are creating/updating or reading Sales Orders via API-M[6] in SAP S/4HANA – where SAP S/4HANA is main Order fulfilment solution.
  • Omni-channel solutions are acquiring via API-M from SAP OPPs (SAP Omnichannel Promotion Pricing) relevant and available on-invoice Promotions.
  • …

Async Request-Reply pattern

Figure 2.-Async Request-Reply

When to use:

  • Near real time needed, but also no real-time for bulk payloads
  • Medium/high volumes
  • Response needed
  • Reliability and near-real time
  • Retry and DMQ/DLQ critical
  • Decoupled needed

Rules:

  • Use broker (AEM – Advanced Event Mesh) for choreography through Topics (incl. dynamic/smart) and Queues, and/or middleware (CPI) with queueing for mapping/orchestration
  • Guaranteed delivery
  • Idempotency is mandatory

Anti-patterns:

  • Building without queueing

Explained:

  • Async Request-Reply is a multi-thread, so System can run in parallel other operations – System sending Request Message will not wait for any Response, before continuing with other operations. The other System may still send back (at some point of time) separate Response Massage, e.g. to update the status of the processing etc. Although the exchange of Request Message and Response Message may be very fast in many cases (almost near-real time), there is no “guarantee”, no “time-out”, and System sending Request Message will not “block” its operations waiting for the Response Message.
  • Requestor (System sending Request Message) does not wait for the response, Responder (System sending Response Message) will send response "at some point of time".
  • No session freezing for the Requestor, Requester can work on other operations.

Examples of use:

  • SAP MDG is providing (Async) one-way synchronization of Material/Product data, BOM, Equipment etc. via AEM[7] Topics/Queues to various Subscribers – RM (Raw Materials) to MES (Manufacturing Execution System) solution, FG (Finish Goods) to Order taking channels – where each will provide confirmation.
  • SAP MDG is providing (Async) two-way synchronization of BP (Business Partner) Vendor/Supplier master data with Ariba – where the other system is sending back the confirmation after processing of the inbound records. This can include CPI[6], but can also be done (exceptionally) directly with DRF processing.
  • SAP S/4HANA is providing (Async) one-way synchronization of bulk delta Customer Hierarchies via CPI with DataStore (or JMS Queue) to Promo solution – where Promo solution is sending back the confirmation of the process batch.
  • …

PubSub pattern

Figure 3. PubSub

When to use:

  • Near real time needed, but also no real-time for bulk payloads
  • High volumes
  • Multiple Providers and Consumers
  • Decoupled needed

Rules:

  • Use broker (AEM – Advanced Event Mesh) for choreography through Topics (incl. dynamic/smart) and Queues
  • Use (optional) dedicated message broker replacing AEM Queues (i.e. Azure Service Bus provides native integration with Microsoft Dynamics 365).
  • Use (optional) middleware (CPI) for message adjustment (i.e. MI in AEM might not be sufficient).
  • Business events are distinct changes in a "state”.
  • Small payloads for Event Notifications, full records for Data Streming.

Anti-patterns:

  • Filtering or adjusting messages in the source for specific target systems – if needed, build smart and use the “power” of dynamic/smart Topics and MI in AEM.

Explained:

  • PubSub (Publish-Subscribe) is Async many-to-many communication between different Systems, decoupling the System that creates messages (the Publisher) from the System that process them (the Subscribers) by using a central intermediary known as a broker.
  • Publishers send messages to a specific Topic in the broker which ensures Subscriber(s) receive a copy of that message, making it highly effective for Event-Driven Architectures
  • Subscriber may be subscribed directly to the Topic or can be connected to a Queue which is subscribed to one or more Topics.

Examples of use:

  • SAP S/4HANA (i.e. via standard CloudEvents or custom add-on messages) and non-SAP “last-mile-delivery” solutions are publishing Event Notifications/Streaming to Omni-channel Order taking apps incl. web and mobile apps – thus providing multi-channel via ICaaS Notification Hub (emails, SMS, social etc.) notifications as well as in-app notifications, to Customers/Consumers and in-house users.
  • CRM solution is providing marketing campaign notifications via ICaaS Notification Hub (emails, SMS, social etc.).
  • SAP S/4HANA (i.e. via add-on “translating” legacy IDOC) is a publishing Data Streaming of Production Order transactional data to MES (Manufacturing Execution System) solutions.
  • …

E(T)L pattern

Figure 4. E(T)L

When to use:

  • No real-time needed
  • Large volume
  • Analytics / reporting use cases

Rules:

  • Use ETL tool or middleware (CPI) with queueing for pulling and pushing data on scheduled intervals
  • Prefer delta over full loads
  • Schedule outside business hours

Anti-pattern:

  • Using batch for operational processes

Explained:

  • E(T)L (Extract-Transform-Load) is a foundational data integration pattern to Extract large datasets from the source system and Load it into the target system.
  • Transformation is an optional process which may be happening in-between extraction and loading or can be happening in the source destination after loading of the datasets.

Examples of use:

  • Extract-and-Load of SAP MDG master data via CPI daily job to non-SAP planning solutions.
  • Extract-and-Load of SAP S/4HANA tables via Azure Data Factory to DWH solution (i.e. Azure DataMesh)
  • …

DB Data Replication pattern

Figure 5. Sync DB Data Replication

When to use:

  • Real-time replication needed
  • Large volumes
  • Full table replication
  • Analytics / reporting use cases

Rules:

  • Use CDC tools (SLT – SAP Landscape Transformation) for instant data replication
  • Prefer delta over full replication

Anti-pattern:

  • Using for transactional processing

Explained:

  • This is DB (Database) table replication of records based on CDC (Change-Data-Capture) change-log.
  • While very powerful tool for “real” time replication, there are limitations – there is limited number od Consumers which can be served, can be intensive on DB server side, bounded with table structures, there are some limitations for tables without change logs or CDS views etc.

Examples of use:

  • Replicating SAP S/4HANA reference data tables via SLT[8] to related SAP MDG tables
  • Replicating SAP S/4HANA tables via SLT to non-SAP DWH solution
  • …

And do apply some “hard” rules…

Do not run-away for apply some rules…. Actually, do it in call cases! Of course, rules may differ from organization to organization, but here are some example:

  • No direct point-to-point integration
  • No bypassing API-M
  • No business logic
  • No backend exposing

Furthermore, thing about the Integration Governance… Setting up the Intgration Principles and defining Integration Pattens may be “easier” part of the overall Integration Guardrails – making it work, well this is usually more challenging…

  • All integrations have clearly defined owners from the respective product teams. This owner is responsible for ensuring the appropriate business context of any integration flow – remember, we do not connect “applications” we integrate “business processes”. Owner provides (business/functional) requests in sufficient (predefined) details, while respective Integration Architects will take over and develop solution (respecting Integration Principles and Appling appropriate Integration Patterns).
  • All developed APIs/EventAPIs must be clearly documented with versioning.
  • All teams must follow Integration Guidelines (i.e. on Performance Testing, Monitoring and Observability). This is cross-platform effort, especially in the Agile teams..
  • Design with backward (and planned forward) compatibility enforced
  • Integrations (no matter which tool is used) in its nature stateless (i.e. avoid extensive mapping, transformations, heavy orchestration rules). While these are old SOA principles, it should be still respected as mush as possible. Modern IPaaS Solutions (like CPI) or brokers (like Kafka with Flink SQL) can do a lot – but is the middleware the right place to keep the business logic? Do we want to hide business logic from the Providers (i.e. “inventing” new in-transit SalesOrder statuses other than those Sap S/4HANA provides)?
  • Security standards (i.e. OAuth).
  • etc.

The decision matrix – when to use what?

Things are (not so) simple? Well, let’s try to build some high-level decision matrix – when to apply which of the Integration Patterns (sorry no diagram, only pseudo-code):

If “Real time needed” then 
    If “Small/medium volumes” then 
        Sync Request-Reply
    Else 
        DB Data Replication
    End If;
Else If “Near real time needed” then
    If “Response needed” then 
        Async Request-Reply
    Else 
        PubSub
    End If;
Else if “No real time needed” then 
    If “Response needed” then 
        Async Request-Reply
    Else if “Multiple Providers and Consumers” then
        PubSub
    Else
        E(T)L
    End If;
End If;

Of course, this is just an example, and we can play with it…

Finally, building our SBBs?

While high-level Integration Patterns are great, this is just a start.

We need to build on top of the high-level Integration Patterns as they do not answer all the questions... As we know “devil is in the details” – depending which Provider(s) and Consumers(s) we are connecting, what Data Objects we are transferring, or what communication protocols we are using (HTTP or AMQP etc.) – “things” may be quite different.

Just a simple example for PubSub:

  • If we publish message from S/4HANA via AEM add-on what will be HTTP attributes we will use for monitoring/observability (i.e. assigning values to “Solace-Message-ID" and/or "Solace-Correlation-ID”) or for partitioning in case our recipient is not on HTTP (i.e. assigning values to "Solace-User-Property-JMSXGroupID”)?
  • Using and designing dynamic/smart topics, what are the requirements?
  • Persistent messages (in queue) or dynamic Topics to Subscriber (i.e. using other tools as a Message Queue like Azure Service Bus)?
  • For persistent design, what is retry and retention policy (time-to-live) and DMQ?
  • Retries and delayed retries in case recipient is not on HTTP?
  • What if the recipient is RDP (REST Delivery Point) on HTTP? We cannot use partitioning, but can we scale connections or consumers on RDP binding?
  • Also, if the recipient is RDP we cannot implement delay retries. What do we do? Is this a must (so we do this with CPI and JMS Queue on top), or can we skip it?
  • etc.

While it can get easier with "simple" Integration Patterns like Sync Request-Reply, it can also get more complex with "heavy” Integration Patterns like Async Request-Reply...

Leadership?

It's not only about how good artifacts (i.e. Integration Patterns or SBBs) we "build”, but it’s mostly about how we collaborate in bringing all this together Each organization will set its own rules – and it may differ significantly. Organizations may observe more or less agile approaches. Or organizations may have specific culture of work.

Still, here are some general areas to address when defining Roles and Responsibilities:

  • Who and how will refine Integration Patterns?
  • Who and how will refine existing or bring new SBBs?
  • Who and how will prepare new Integration requirements?
  • How do we ensure Integration Principles (i.e. REUSE) is observed?
  • How do we ensure Integration Patterns and SBBs are applied?
  • Who does functional design?
  • Who does technical design?
  • Who will do different testing phases (SIT, UAT, performance testing etc)
  • Who and how will implement monitoring and observability?
  • When and how do we pass the Integration Service to support?
  • What is the definition of ready?
  • What is the definition of done?
  • etc.

At the end, putting all this together is about leadership – and no, I do not say it’s "one person" – it’s about how do we make "leadership happen" in all phases. Clearly this cannot be only EA or SA doing it all. We need to have all the "integration artifacts” make sense – it cannot be "disconnected” from the reality. Having delivery team members involved early enough is an absolute must.

Integration Guardrails are more than just Integration Patterns – it's more than just Integration Architecture as well. Guardrails are defining the “boundaries" we follow when “integrating everything with everyone”. Architecture is just one “piece” of the puzzle – but this puzzle has many pieces.  

Conclusion

The main purpose of this article is to:

  • Connect the “dots” from the past (previous articles and terminology) with new “simplified” view and (high-level) patterns.
  • Explain that we can leverage from the past experiences and continue with our SAP Integration Suite in future – using of course Advance Event Mesh much more, but not neglecting the usage of Cloud Integration and API-M, as it all “fits” our future needs.

Can we build "fully" decoupled and loosely-coupled integrations around ISA-M with SAP Integration Suite in (near) future? What will SAP Business Data Cloud bring as per “new” Integration Patterns around Data Products? And what are AI and MCP really bringing in the integration Patterns?

Many questions, but future is not “certain” always. Maybe in few years (or less) I will be refreshing the Integration Patterns article with some new “buzz-word”…

entry.title: SAP Integration Suite Licensing: A Practical Guide for Businesses and Architects
entry.content:
Introduction

Within the SAP ecosystem, developers benefit from extensive documentation and technical tutorials. However, business leaders, enterprise architects, procurement teams, and startups often struggle to find clear guidance on licensing, pricing, and commercial models—particularly for SAP Integration Suite.

This blog bridges that gap by offering a practical, business-focused overview of SAP Integration Suite licensing, along with real-world case studies that illustrate how organizations can select the most suitable commercial model.

Why Licensing Information Is Hard to Find

Unlike technical documentation, commercial details are not widely publicized. Key reasons include:

1. Tailored Pricing Models

SAP solutions are customised based on:

  • Organization size and industry
  • Integration volumes and complexity
  • Geographic presence
  • Compliance requirements
  • Existing SAP investments

2. Sales-Led Engagement Model

Licensing information is typically provided through:

  • SAP account executives
  • Authorized SAP partners
  • Commercial proposals and Statements of Work

3. Consumption-Based Cloud Economics

SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP) follows a consumption-based model where costs depend on usage metrics such as:

  • Integration runtime capacity
  • Messages processed
  • API calls and events
  • Compute and memory utilization
  • Additional capabilities like B2B Integration and API Management

4. Rapid Evolution of SAP Offerings

SAP frequently enhances its cloud offerings, making static pricing references less reliable over time.

Overview of SAP Integration Suite Commercial Models

1. Free Tier

Best For: Developers, students, and innovation teams

Purpose: Learning, experimentation, and prototyping

Benefits:

  • No cost
  • Ideal for proofs of concept
  • Hands-on experience

Limitations:

  • Restricted resources
  • Not intended for production use

2. Pay-As-You-Go (PAYG)

Best For: Startups, SMEs, and organizations with unpredictable workloads

Benefits:

  • No upfront commitment
  • Pay only for what you consume
  • Rapid scalability and flexibility

Considerations:

  • Requires cost governance
  • Expenses increase with scale

3. Cloud Platform Enterprise Agreement (CPEA)

Best For: Large enterprises adopting multiple SAP BTP services

Benefits:

  • Prepaid cloud credits
  • Flexibility across SAP BTP services
  • Volume-based discounts
  • Centralized governance

Considerations:

  • Requires upfront financial commitment
  • Needs consumption planning

4. Subscription-Based Licensing

Best For: Organizations with stable and predictable workloads

Benefits:

  • Predictable costs
  • Simplified budgeting
  • Guaranteed capacity

Considerations:

  • Less flexibility compared to consumption models
  • Potential risk of underutilization

5. RISE with SAP

Best For: Organizations adopting SAP S/4HANA Cloud as part of digital transformation

Benefits:

  • Bundled services under a single contract
  • Simplified vendor management
  • Accelerated cloud adoption

Considerations:

  • Less granular pricing visibility
  • Best suited for SAP-centric landscapes

Decision Matrix: Choosing the Right Model

Business Scenario

Recommended Model

Learning and experimentation

Startups building their first integrations

Pay-As-You-Go

SMEs with growing integration needs

PAYG transitioning to CPEA

System integrators and consulting firms

PAYG for projects; CPEA for internal use

Key Cost Drivers for SAP Integration Suite

Cost Driver

Business Impact

Number of integrations

Influences runtime capacity

Message volume

Major contributor to consumption costs

API calls

Impacts API Management usage

B2B/EDI capabilities

Adds specialized costs

Data transformation complexity

High availability and scalability

Real-World Case Studies

Case Study 1: Startup Integrating SaaS Applications

Industry: HR Technology Startup

Challenge: Integrate a cloud-based HR platform with SAP S/4HANA for clients.

Solution: Pay-As-You-Go model.

Implementation:

  • Connected Salesforce, SAP S/4HANA, and SuccessFactors.
  • Leveraged API Management and Cloud Integration.
  • Scaled gradually based on customer demand.

Outcome:

  • Zero upfront investment.
  • Faster time-to-market.
  • Controlled operational expenses.

Why PAYG Was Ideal:

  • Unpredictable workloads.
  • Need for agility and cost efficiency.

Case Study 2: Manufacturing Enterprise Modernizing Legacy Systems

Industry: Global Manufacturing

Challenge: Replace point-to-point integrations across SAP ECC, Ariba, and third-party logistics providers.

Solution: Cloud Platform Enterprise Agreement (CPEA).

Implementation:

  • Standardized enterprise integrations using SAP Integration Suite.
  • Enabled EDI and API-based partner connectivity.
  • Utilized BTP credits across multiple services.

Outcome:

  • Reduced integration complexity.
  • Improved supply chain visibility.
  • Optimized costs through prepaid credits.

Why CPEA Was Ideal:

  • Large-scale, enterprise-wide adoption.
  • Need for flexibility across multiple BTP services.

Case Study 3: Retail Chain Managing Seasonal Demand

Industry: Retail and E-Commerce

Challenge: Handle fluctuating integration volumes during festive and seasonal peaks.

Solution: Pay-As-You-Go model.

Implementation:

  • Integrated SAP Commerce Cloud with logistics and payment gateways.
  • Scaled integrations during peak sales periods.

Outcome:

  • Cost optimization during off-peak seasons.
  • Elastic scalability during high demand.

Why PAYG Was Ideal:

  • Variable workloads and seasonal spikes.

Case Study 4: Banking Institution Requiring Predictable Costs

Industry: Banking and Financial Services

Challenge: Ensure secure, compliant, and stable integrations across core banking systems.

Solution: Subscription-Based Licensing.

Implementation:

  • Integrated SAP and non-SAP systems with strict governance.
  • Ensured regulatory compliance and high availability.

Outcome:

  • Predictable budgeting and financial planning.
  • Stable, mission-critical operations.

Why Subscription Was Ideal:

  • Consistent transaction volumes.
  • Strong compliance requirements.

Case Study 5: Enterprise Migrating to SAP S/4HANA Cloud

Industry: Professional Services

Challenge: Transform legacy systems while migrating to SAP S/4HANA Cloud.

Solution: RISE with SAP.

Implementation:

  • Leveraged pre-packaged integrations and clean-core principles.
  • Enabled seamless connectivity across cloud applications.

Outcome:

  • Simplified vendor and contract management.
  • Accelerated digital transformation.

Why RISE with SAP Was Ideal:

  • Unified approach to ERP modernization and integration.

A Typical Adoption Journey

Most organizations follow this path:

Free Tier → Pay-As-You-Go → CPEA or Subscription → RISE with SAP

This approach enables businesses to:

  • Validate use cases
  • Optimize investments
  • Scale efficiently
  • Reduce financial risks

Essential Questions to Ask SAP or Partners

Before selecting a commercial model, consider asking:

  1. What metrics determine Integration Suite costs?
  2. Which capabilities are included in the license?
  3. How are non-production environments billed?
  4. Are there volume discounts available?
  5. What governance tools exist for cost monitoring?
  6. Can the commercial model be converted later?
  7. What is the estimated total cost of ownership over three years?
  8. How does pricing scale as the organization grows?

Recommended Resources

  • SAP Discovery Center 
  • SAP BTP Pricing Calculator
  • SAP Help Portal
  • SAP Community Blogs and Q&A
  • SAP Learning Hub and openSAP
  • Authorized SAP Partners and Account Executives

Key Takeaways

  • Pay-As-You-Go is a licensing model—not a license-free option.
  • CPEA provides flexibility and cost optimization for enterprises.
  • Subscription models offer predictable costs for stable workloads.
  • RISE with SAP simplifies ERP-led transformations.
  • Architects must align technical architecture with commercial strategy.
  • Understanding licensing early prevents costly redesigns later.

Conclusion

While developers benefit from extensive technical guidance, businesses and architects often lack clarity around licensing and pricing. By understanding SAP Integration Suite’s commercial models, organizations can make informed decisions that align technology investments with business goals.

Selecting the right licensing model ensures scalability, cost efficiency, and long-term success in the cloud integration journey.

Call to Action

Have you implemented SAP Integration Suite using PAYG, CPEA, Subscription, or RISE with SAP? Share your experiences and insights in the comments to help the SAP Community learn and grow together.

Thank you for reading!
