entry.title: SAP Business Data Cloud: What Actually Changes When S/4HANA Data Becomes a Data Product
entry.content:
What SAP actually changed: SAP becomes the producer

Data products are not new; the data-mesh community has argued for them since around 2019. What SAP did in Business Data Cloud (BDC) is structural: for SAP sources, SAP itself becomes the producer.

SAP-managed data products ship with the platform. They are pre-built extractions from S/4HANA and other SAP applications, landed and refreshed by SAP-managed pipelines into the BDC storage layer (HDLF), and published to the catalog with their business semantics attached. You do not build the extraction or its base semantics. You activate them, and build only the logic that is genuinely yours on top, which moves your scarce engineering effort from plumbing to differentiation. Where data-team bandwidth is the binding constraint, and for most organizations it is, that is the whole game.

This is not "only SAP data." There are three doors into the same governed catalog. Only the first is gated by an application purchase.

 

Why “zero-copy” is a fact, not a slogan

The foundation stores data products as open columnar files (Parquet, managed as Delta tables) in a managed object store built on SAP HANA Data Lake Files (HDLF). File-based is the key phrase. A warehouse locks data inside a proprietary format, so the only way to share it is to export a copy. An object store keeps data as open files in a bucket, and open files can be read by many engines at once without anyone copying anything.

This is the lakehouse principle applied inside SAP: one physical copy in open Delta format, read by SAP Datasphere, SAP Databricks, and SAP HANA Cloud through a shared catalog. Inside the BDC boundary, that means produce once and consume across all three engines without duplicating the data. One copy, many readers, that is the mechanism the market calls "zero-copy."

The full pipeline: how data actually lands in HDLF

For technical audiences, here is the honest end-to-end. CDS views are the extraction interface throughout, but the pipeline runs in two contexts. In the SAP-managed context, SAP owns standard, SAP-released CDS views built on the One Domain Model, its cross-application semantic model that keeps core entities consistent. In the customer-managed context, you create or identify the CDS entity yourself: a standard view, an extended or Z-CDS view, a custom business object, or a table. The same physical machinery moves both, and that machinery is what the rest of this section walks through.

 

 

 

Extraction at a glance, by source system

 

Cloud S/4HANA activates SAP-managed data products directly; everything else, on-prem S/4HANA, ECC, and non-SAP, enters through the customer-managed door. The source differs, the entry point does not: CDS views over the Cloud Connector for on-prem, extractors and tables via a Datasphere connection for ECC, database and file connections for third-party. Whatever the origin, one Replication Flow performs the universal physical write into HDLF as Delta Parquet, landing in a single governed catalog.

 

One product, end to end, and back

Follow a single product from source to intelligence and back. It leaves S/4HANA through SAP-managed CDS extraction and lands in the BDC foundation as governed Delta files. It appears in the catalog carrying its schema, semantics, and lineage: the "app store" moment where you browse before you install. The customer activates it, making it consumable.

From there the same single product serves everything. Datasphere models it; SAP Analytics Cloud plans and reports on it; and when a data-science team wants it, it is shared to SAP Databricks over Delta Sharing, appearing in Unity Catalog as a mounted table while the bytes stay in the foundation. What crosses the share is the table and its column-level meaning: names, types, keys, and comments, so the data scientist sees labeled, described columns rather than naked ones. What does not cross is the multidimensional model or the source-side access controls, measures, hierarchies, and data-access rules live in Datasphere and SAC, not in the shared file, and are re-established on the consumer side. Zero-copy is real at the boundary; meaning travels at the column level, not the model level.

When the loop closes, the data product is published back into BDC as a new governed data product through a federated remote share, live and zero-copy, not a physical import.

One honest boundary

Good advisory work separates what a platform will show from what it will guarantee. So, plainly: Delta Sharing transports tables, not multidimensional models. Measures, hierarchies, and data-access controls do not survive the protocol and must be re-established on the consuming side. The semantics that carry over are the structural ones (keys, column names, comments, data types), not the full analytic model. Say this up front and you will be trusted; let people discover it later and you will not.

Go Deeper On Delta Sharing: 

https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-sap/customer-managed-data-products-in-sap-bdc-what-really-happens-when-your/ba-p/14394675

The economics: what actually burns capacity

Most confusion about BDC cost comes from collapsing three things that are actually separate. Hold them apart and the economics stop being mysterious. This is the distinction solution architects and commercial teams have to be able to explain to a customer.

Illustrative split from a small worked example. Exact mix depends on data volume, refresh frequency, and workloads run.

The single most misunderstood point in the whole model: intelligent content does not consume capacity units. You license the application, but what burns capacity is the data products and infrastructure underneath it. Switching on more applications barely moves the meter. Cost follows the workloads you actually run on your data (provisioning, refresh, queries, and any optional ML in Databricks), not the number of applications you own.

Why this matters now

The reason the industry is talking about governed data products in 2026 is not nostalgia for data-mesh theory. It is AI. Agents and copilots fail in production mostly because they lack business context: they do not know that this table means settlement, or that this field is a posted invoice. A governed data product is that context, delivered with the data. The same foundation that ends your dashboard disagreements is what makes your S/4HANA data trustworthy enough to hand to an AI.

So the shift from pipelines to products is really two shifts at once. It retires a decade of brittle, unowned extractions and their hidden maintenance cost. And it builds the governed, meaningful foundation the next wave of enterprise AI actually requires, data that is AI-ready because it is governed and meaningful, not merely moved faster.

That is what changes when your S/4HANA data becomes a product, not a pipeline.

SAP Enterprise Architecture Designer SAP Datasphere SAP Databricks SAP Analytics Cloud, connectivity SAP Business Data Cloud

entry.title: Call to Action for SAP CPI / Integration Suite - Restrict Usage to Supported Frameworks & Libraries
entry.content:
Below check scans will be effective from July 26th onwards for both CPI and Integration Suite tenants.

Introduction

SAP Integration Suite allows developers to use Groovy scripts to implement custom integration logic. While Groovy scripting provides tremendous flexibility, it also introduces a risk: developers may unknowingly use internal, unsupported, or restricted frameworks and libraries that are not guaranteed to work across platform updates.

To address this, SAP has introduced the "Restrict usage to supported frameworks and libraries" guideline in the Integration Assessment capabilities. This guideline helps identify potentially problematic dependencies within Groovy scripts and encourages developers to use only supported APIs and libraries.

In this blog, we will explore why this guideline is important, the frameworks it detects, common pitfalls, and best practices for building upgrade-safe Groovy scripts.

This guideline helps identify the use of internal, unsupported, or restricted classes and libraries in groovy scripts. Using unsupported frameworks can result in runtime failures, upgrade incompatibilities, maintenance challenges, and unexpected behavior after software updates.

The guideline scans both versions of groovy scripts version 1 and version 2.

No automatic fix is provided for this; you must manually replace or remove unsupported implementations.

 

The guideline detects usage of unsupported frameworks & class groups, including:

  • OSGi (org.osgi.framework.*, org.osgi.service.event.*)

  • Quartz (org.quartz.*)

  • Spring (org.springframework*)

  • HikariCP (com.zaxxer.hikari.*)

  • Groovy SQL (groovy.sql.*)

  • Saxon (net.sf.saxon.*)

  • Selected Apache Camel internal classes (org.apache.camel.*)

 
Call to Action : Refactor the script to use supported alternatives.

Final Thoughts

By avoiding internal frameworks such as OSGi, Apache Camel internals, Quartz, Spring, HikariCP, Groovy SQL, and Saxon, developers can significantly reduce the risk of runtime failures after platform updates. Instead, leverage SAP-supported APIs, adapters, mappings, and integration services designed specifically for Cloud Integration/Integration Suite.
 
Doing so will result in cleaner integrations, easier maintenance, and a smoother upgrade experience for years to come.

entry.title: How We Built Rapid Migration: Simplifying SAP Integration Suite Migration from Neo to Cloud Foundry
entry.content:
Introduction

As organizations continue modernizing their integration landscapes, migrating from the SAP Integration Suite Neo environment to Cloud Foundry has become an important step toward adopting a more scalable and cloud-native platform.

During our work on SAP Integration Suite migration projects, we observed that many customers had built large integration landscapes over several years. These environments often contained hundreds of integration packages, custom integration flows, certificates, security artifacts, value mappings, variables, and other configuration objects that were critical to business operations.

Although SAP provides the destination platform, the migration journey itself was often challenging. Teams spent significant time identifying dependencies, validating migrated artifacts, tracking migration progress, and ensuring nothing was overlooked. Much of this work was managed manually using spreadsheets and repeated validation exercises, making migration both time-consuming and prone to errors.

These challenges led us to build RapidMigrate, a solution on SAP Business Technology Platform (SAP BTP) that helps migration teams analyze, execute, monitor, and validate Neo to Cloud Foundry migrations through a single application.

Current Challenges

From our experience, the biggest challenge wasn't moving artifacts—it was managing the migration process itself.

Some common challenges included:

  • Limited visibility into migration readiness
  • Understanding dependencies between integration artifacts
  • Manual migration tracking using spreadsheets
  • Validating migrated content across environments
  • Monitoring deployment progress
  • Coordinating migration activities across teams

As migration projects became larger, these challenges increased project timelines and operational risk.

Our Approach

To address these challenges, we built RapidMigrate on SAP Business Technology Platform (SAP BTP) as a centralized migration analytics and governance solution for SAP Integration Suite modernization.

Instead of switching between multiple tools, migration teams can perform the entire migration lifecycle through one application—from analyzing the existing landscape to monitoring migration execution and validating migrated artifacts.

Our objective was simple: to reduce manual effort, improve operational visibility, and provide migration teams with greater confidence throughout the migration journey.

RapidMigrate is built on SAP Business Technology Platform using SAP Build Work Zone, SAP UI5, SAP Cloud Application Programming Model (CAP), SAP Destination Service, and SAP Application Logging Service. This architecture enables secure connectivity, centralized governance, and scalable migration execution.

 

Key Features and Benefits

1. Integration Analytics Dashboard

One of the first steps in any migration project is understanding the existing integration landscape.

RapidMigrate provides a centralized analytics dashboard that offers complete visibility into integration packages, deployment readiness, sender and receiver systems, certificates, variables, value mappings, and other migration artifacts.

Interactive charts and dashboards help migration teams quickly assess migration readiness, monitor progress, and identify dependencies before migration begins.

 

 

2. Migration Content Management

Neo to Cloud Foundry migration involves multiple configuration artifacts that need to be migrated in a structured and controlled manner.

RapidMigrate provides a centralized Migration Content Management module that organizes migration activities into structured components such as Certificates, Data Stores, Variables, Security Artifacts, Custom Tags, Number Range Objects, Value Mappings, and Custom Content.

This structured approach simplifies migration planning while improving execution and governance.

3. Automated Migration Workflows

Migrating integration artifacts manually can be repetitive and time-consuming, particularly in large integration landscapes.

RapidMigrate automates migration workflows for multiple SAP Integration Suite artifacts, reducing manual effort while maintaining consistency and accuracy throughout the migration process.

Migration teams can execute controlled migrations while monitoring progress and validating results from a centralized interface.

4. Migration Validation and Comparison

Successful migration is not only about moving artifacts but also verifying that every required component has been migrated correctly.

RapidMigrate provides post-migration comparison capabilities that compare Neo and Cloud Foundry environments, identify missing or mismatched artifacts, and validate migration completeness.

This gives organizations greater confidence before production deployment.

5. Migration Governance

Migration projects require continuous monitoring to ensure visibility, governance, and traceability throughout the migration lifecycle.

RapidMigrate provides centralized dashboards, migration tracking, dependency analysis, and deployment monitoring, enabling teams to manage migration activities and maintain governance throughout the migration lifecycle.

6. Artifact Migration Modules

RapidMigrate provides dedicated migration modules for key SAP Integration Suite artifacts, including Certificates, Data Stores, Variables, Security Artifacts, Access Policies, Number Range Objects, Custom Tags, Custom Content, and Value Mappings. Each module offers a guided workflow to review existing configurations, execute controlled migrations, and validate results, helping teams migrate artifacts consistently while reducing manual effort and maintaining governance throughout the migration process.

 

 

 

 

7. Built-in User Guide

To simplify the migration experience, RapidMigrate includes a built-in user guide that provides step-by-step instructions, best practices, and guidance for each stage of the migration process. This helps both new and experienced users understand the workflow, execute migration activities more efficiently, and follow a consistent approach throughout the project.

Business Value

Based on our project experience, RapidMigrate has helped simplify migration activities in several practical ways:

  • Reduced manual effort through automated migration workflows.
  • Improved visibility into migration readiness and deployment progress.
  • Simplified dependency analysis across integration artifacts.
  • Increased confidence through post-migration validation.

Enabled teams to focus on business outcomes rather than administrative activities

Conclusion

Migrating SAP Integration Suite landscapes from Neo to Cloud Foundry is more than a technical upgrade—it is an opportunity to modernize integration operations.

From our experience, having centralized visibility and automation throughout the migration lifecycle made migration projects easier to manage and reduced the effort required for validation and tracking.

By bringing migration analysis, execution, governance, and validation into a single platform, RapidMigrate helps organizations modernize their SAP Integration Suite landscapes more efficiently while improving operational visibility, governance, and confidence throughout the migration lifecycle.

entry.title: Top 5 Integration Anti-Patterns I See in SAP Projects
entry.content:
Top 5 Integration Anti-Patterns I See in SAP Projects

Introduction:

Over time, working on SAP Integration Suite (CPI) implementations across different projects, I’ve noticed a pattern — many integration issues don’t come from platform limitations, but from the way we design and build our iFlows.

This post is a collection of 5 common anti-patterns I’ve either encountered or personally made while developing SAP integrations. These are not theoretical mistakes, but practical ones that impact maintainability, scalability, and long-term stability.

If you are working with CPI in real-world enterprise scenarios, chances are you’ve seen at least a few of these — or might be unknowingly heading toward them.

Real-world problem use-cases with solution:

Here are a few patterns I keep running into:

Anti-Pattern 1:  CPI behaving like a backend system storing data, holding logic, doing more than it should.

Script: SC_AllocateAndSequenceDeliveries.groovy: 

import com.sap.gateway.ip.core.customdev.util.Message
import com.sap.it.api.ITApiFactory
import com.sap.it.api.asdk.datastore.*
import groovy.json.*
def Message processData(Message message) {
def svc = ITApiFactory.getService(DataStoreService.class, null)
def req = new JsonSlurper().parseText(message.getBody(String))
// --- CPI is the system of record for available quantity ---

def entry = svc.get("DS_ALLOCATION_LEDGER", req.material + "_" + req.plant)
def ledger = entry ? new JsonSlurper().parseText(new String(entry.getDataAsArray()))
: [available: 0, allocated: 0, lastSeq: 0]

// --- CPI decides the business outcome ---
def granted
if (ledger.available >= req.qtyRequested) {
granted = req.qtyRequested
req.status = "FULL"
} else if (ledger.available > 0) {
granted = ledger.available // partial allocation decision
req.status = "PARTIAL"
req.backorderQty = req.qtyRequested - granted
} else {
granted = 0
req.status = "REJECTED"
}

// --- CPI mints the business document number ---
ledger.lastSeq = ledger.lastSeq + 1
req.allocationNo = "ALC-" + req.plant + "-" +
String.format("%08d", ledger.lastSeq)

ledger.available -= granted
ledger.allocated += granted
ledger.lastUpdatedBy = message.getProperty("SAP_MessageProcessingLogID")

def bean = new DataBean(); bean.setDataAsArray(JsonOutput.toJson(ledger).bytes)
def cfg = new DataConfig()
cfg.setStoreName("DS_ALLOCATION_LEDGER")
cfg.setId(req.material + "_" + req.plant)
cfg.setOverwrite(true)
svc.put(bean, cfg)

message.setBody(JsonOutput.toJson(req))
return message
}

The trouble this caused: The available/allocated quantity data and the decision now live in a middleware store which becomes a second source of truth, with no clear ownership or reconciliation mechanism with S/4HANA.

Solution: We started pushing logic back to source/target systems and kept CPI focused on orchestration.

Anti-Pattern 2: Everything built synchronously. One delay downstream, and suddenly the whole chain feels it.

Business Requirement: HR completes a new hire in SuccessFactors, using CPI, the record is sent to SAP Payroll. Payroll generates the employee number and sends it back.

Why will asynchronous flow work perfectly? The new joiner starts in future, and nothing happens today. Payroll doesn’t run until 25th. So, whenever the records are created, the business outcome is identical.

Why was a synchronous flow built anyway? The HR demanded that the employee number must appear on screen before HR user closes the hire, so that they know that the process has worked.

The trouble this caused: Payroll is down one morning. The integration times out and the HR sees an error. But Payroll did create the record. It was just slow in answering and by the time it answered, the connection was closed. HR sees an error, assumes that employee number wasn’t created and reruns the process. So, the record got created twice.

Solution: Build an asynchronous integration in which failed transactions sit in a queue and can be retried if required. As for the employee number, it is sent back via a different interface using CPI. This reduced cascading failures immediately.

Anti-Pattern 3: Hardcoded values everywhere: Endpoints, credentials, logic.

SC_ApplyBusinessRules_Pricing.groovy — rules hardcoded in script

def Message processData(Message message) {
def plant = message.getProperty("Plant")
def discount = 0
if (plant == "1010" || plant == "1020") discount = 12.5
else if (plant == "2010") discount = 7.0
else if (plant == "3010" &&
message.getProperty("CustGrp") == "Z1") discount = 15.0
// + 240 lines accreted over three years
message.setProperty("Discount", discount)
return message
}

The trouble this caused: A rate change is a code change. DEV→QA→PRD transport plus CAB. Business can’t see or audit the rules. Nobody knows who changed 12.5 to 13.

Solution: VM_Plant_Discount Value Mapping artifact, externalized parameters, or a lookup. Script does dispatch, not policy. Thus, Changes became controlled, not chaotic.

Anti-Pattern 4: Manual transport between tenants.

No clear trace of what moved where.
Even if you try very hard, you won’t be able to maintain uniformity and sync between Dev, QA, Pre-Prod and Prod if you are importing/exporting integration objects and not using TMS.

The trouble this caused:

  • Wrong version can be moved.
  • Dependencies (value mappings, scripts, security material) can be missed.
  • Different configurations differ across tenants.
  • Manual approach is inefficient.

Solution: Enforced transport via TMS only. No exceptions. Auditability improved overnight.

Anti-Pattern 5: Interfaces no one owns anymore still running and deployed.

The trouble this caused:

  • nobody knows whether it is still required
  • nobody knows who should troubleshoot it
  • obsolete interfaces continue consuming operational/monitoring resources
  • changes to connected systems can unexpectedly break them

Solution: Did a full inventory + clean-up.
If no owner/use case → removed. Landscape became lighter instantly. 

Final Thought:

SAP Integration Suite is a powerful platform, but like any tool, its effectiveness depends on how we use it.
Avoiding these anti-patterns is less about following strict rules and more about adopting the right mindset — designing integrations that are clean, reusable, and maintainable over time. Many of these mistakes are easy to make, especially under project pressure, but recognizing them early can save significant effort later.

I’m curious to hear from others in the community — what integration challenges or anti-patterns have you encountered in your projects? Feel free to share your experiences or questions in the comments.

entry.title: One More iFlow? When Integration Becomes a Product
entry.content:
Introduction:

The goal of this document is not to build fewer iFlows — it is to stop building project-specific integrations every time a new requirement arrives.

It includes practical examples of how we can turn integration capabilities into reusable products using SAP Cloud Integration and API Management, so that new projects become consumers of existing capabilities rather than starting another integration from scratch.

Treating an integration (iFlow in SAP Cloud Platform Integration) as a product means it is:

  1. Discoverable 
  2. Reusable
  3. Governed 
  4. Has consumers 
  5. Versioned & measurable 

And as these APIs mature into products, usage analytics can provide another dimension: understanding who is consuming a capability, how much they are consuming, and what value it delivers. For APIs exposed to external consumers or partners, this can eventually open the door to usage-based commercial models and new revenue opportunities.

The obligation and the hidden cost of quick integrations:

Every project has a deadline - Once the development is done, testing completed and interface works - everyone moves on. The problem starts when this becomes the default strategy for every project.
One requirement leads to one iFlow. Another project brings another requirement — so we build another iFlow. And because each interface works, we rarely stop to question the bigger picture.

Without a clear integration strategy from the beginning, project timelines naturally drive architecture.

But integrations don't disappear when the project ends. They stay — along with every design decision made under project pressure. Over time, we may end up with a landscape that is no longer scalable, reusable, or easy to govern.

Making the shift:

Tools that help in achieving this approach:

  1. SAP API Business Hub: Ensures consistency across APIs and encourages reuse instead of reinvention.
  2. SAP Cloud Integration: Orchestration, Mapping and Protocol mediation.
  3. SAP API-M: Manage Security, rate limiting & quotas, analytics, monitoring & versioning.
  4. SAP API Portal: APIs become discoverable assets where developers can subscribe and test. Also, documentation is centralized.

Problem Case: Employee Master Data

Like many, one of the organizations I worked for used SAP SuccessFactors as the system of record for employee information.

Different applications need employee data for completely different business processes:

  • Onboarding platform → employee identity, job, manager, department, location
  • Recruitment / internal mobility → employee profile, position, organization data
  • Payroll → employment, compensation and organizational information
  • Leave management → employee ID, employment status, work schedule, organization
  • Asset management → employee ID, name, department, location, manager
  • Corporate directory / IAM → identity and organizational attributes
  • Analytics / data platforms → broader employee master data

The traditional project-driven response is usually: “This application needs employee data. Let's build an iFlow.”  And then another project comes along: “This application also needs employee data. Let's build another iFlow.”  And soon, we lose control.

Individually, every interface may be perfectly valid. Collectively, however, we have created multiple consumers directly dependent on SuccessFactors APIs and multiple implementations of essentially the same business capability.

Project driven Integration model

Product driven Integration model

 Expose master data as enterprise capability

While architecting the interface, make sure you expose the API and do not take the responsibility of pushing the data to different downstream apps.

API-M policies should control access and consumption. They should not be used to decide which SuccessFactors fields each application gets.

Use-Case 1: Same data, multiple applications

Solution Design:

One CI capability + one API resource + multiple API-M consumers.

Build one IFlow in CPI which is used to fetch, orchestrate and transform required set of fields from SF OData APIs. Create Employee API Product on API-M and expose to relevant downstream applications after enforcing required authorization, policy, scope, rate limiting, quota etc.

DO NOT provide both applications the same credentials and maintain them as separate entities. If one application is compromised, we can revoke it’s credentials without impacting the other application.

Example:

API Request: 

GET /api/v1/employees/100245

API Response:

{
"employeeId": "100245",
"firstName": "Bipasha",
"lastName": "Ray",
"department": "IT",
"location": "Dubai",
"manager": "Walter Dough"
}

Both Onboarding and Asset Management consume the same API, using separate client identities and credentials in API-M. The consuming applications do not need to know whether the data is sourced from PerPerson, EmpJob, or another SuccessFactors API.

Use-Case 2: Different data, different applications

Solution Design: Different API resources/CI implementations, but under the same Employee API Product.

Create separate CI implementations where the underlying business capability or data contract is genuinely different and expose them as resources under the same Employee API Product. Formulate the endpoints that is self-explanatory of the business purpose. This will ensure that if tomorrow a third application needs the same employment data as Payroll, it reuses the existing API. You don't build IFlow C.

E.g.: GET /employees/{id} --> Basic employee data – IFlow A

GET /employees/{id}/employment --> Employment data – IFlow B

For every consumer, enforce unique authorization, policy, scope, rate limiting, quota etc. in API-M.

Use-Case 3: Same data, different security requirements

Solution Design: Same API. Same CI. Different API-M policies.

Assuming the same set of data is to be exposed for internal HR applications and external SaaS applications.                                   

Internal HR application → can call it freely within agreed limits.                                                                 

External SaaS application → requires stronger authentication, tighter rate limits, IP restrictions, etc.

Both applications consume the same Employee API, but API-M identifies them using separate client identities and applies different policies. For example, the external application can be restricted through tighter quotas, rate limits and IP restrictions without changing the CI implementation.

Use-Case 4: SuccessFactors changes underneath

Today you are using Compound Employee API and later you decide to start using OData entities - PerPerson, EmpEmployment, EmpJob and User.     

Solution Design: We change the implementation in CI, while the consumer continues calling the same API Product exposed via API-M.

Because the consumer is dependent on the enterprise API contract rather than the underlying SuccessFactors API, this backend change does not necessarily require changes in every consuming application.

Final Thought

An integration should not be considered successful simply because the message reached the target system.

The real measure of success is what happens after the project is over — can another application discover it, consume it securely, reuse it, and evolve with it without requiring us to build yet another interface?

For teams adopting this approach, the first question for a new requirement changes from “Which iFlow should we build?” to “Does this capability already exist, and if not, should we build it for reuse?”

That is the shift from Integration as a Project to Integration as a Product.

Transition -Overview

A Sales Cloud & Service Cloud V1-to-V2 integration transition typically involves three related but distinct activities:

  • Rationalising the existing V1 integration landscape.
  • Adapting or redesigning integrations for the V2 API and business object model.
  • Modernising the Integration Suite platform where required — including Neo-to-Cloud Foundry migration.

End-to-end transition stages:

A structured programme moves through following eight stages.  

Stage

Description

1 Inventory

Identify all V1 integrations, their dependencies, and owners.

2 Rationalise

Classify each interface: Standard content | Custom rebuild | Redesign | Retire.

3 Map APIs

Map V1 business objects, APIs, fields, and events to V2 equivalents.

4 Platform Migration

*Where applicable, migrate Integration Suite from Neo to Cloud Foundry.

5 Build / Adapt

Deploy standard packages; rebuild or redesign custom interfaces.

6 Test

Connectivity, API, mapping, functional, volume, resilience, and E2E testing.

7 Cutover

Disable V1 traffic, enable V2, synchronise delta data, reconcile.

8 Hypercare

Monitor, reconcile, stabilise, and retire V1.

1. Identify the V1 Integrations and Build Your Transition Inventory

Before transition of any individual iFlow, create a complete inventory of the existing V1 integration landscape. In mature C4C implementations, integration is a key migration risk, as undocumented point-to-point integrations may depend on knowledge held by individuals who are no longer available.

Organize the integrations by business process rather than by technical interface, as this will better align with V2 scoping, migration planning, and cutover activities.

Process groupings

Master Data Replication:  Business Partner (Account / Individual Customer), Contact / BP Relationship, Product, Employee, Territory / Sales Organisation hierarchies, Company.

Sales Processes:  Lead-to-Opportunity, Quote, Sales Order replication to ERP / S/4HANA, Pricing, Product Catalogue, Sales status updates.

Service Processes:  Ticket / Case creation and update, Service Order / Confirmation to ERP & S/4 HANA, Equipment / Installed Base / Registered Product synchronisation.

Cross-Channel / Experience:  Marketing platform sync,  Customer portals, Self-service applications, Chat / email channel integrations.

Analytics and Downstream:  SAP Datasphere feeds, Data Warehouse, BI extracts, custom reporting pulls.

Middleware / Utility:  Attachment handling, custom REST APIs consumed by non-SAP systems.

Classify each iFlow

  1. Standard —  A pre-packaged V2 integration package from the Business Accelerator Hub covers this scenario. Adopt rather than rebuild.
  2. Custom (Adapt) —  The business process is still valid, but the V1 implementation must be redesigned for the V2 API model.
  3. Redesign —  The V1 business object or process has materially changed in V2. Revisit the integration architecture before any development.
  4. Retire —  The process no longer exists or is now handled natively by V2. Do not migrate; decommission.

2.Build Sales Cloud & Service Cloud V1 → V2 API and Business Object Gap Matrix

This is one of the most important and most frequently skipped early activities. Do not create a mapping based only on entity names. Validate business object semantics, relationships, lifecycle, keys, statuses, partner functions, and ownership model before any development begins.

3.NEO to Cloud Foundry: Integration Suite Migration Plan

If Integration Suite is still running on the Neo environment, the Neo-to-Cloud Foundry migration should be treated as a coordinated but separate platform workstream — not the same migration as V1-to-V2. They touch the same iFlows and the same test cycles, so planning them together is essential. SAP Business Technology Platform, Neo environment will sunset on December 31, 2028, subject to terms of customer or partner contracts. For more information, see SAP Note 3351844 

NEO → Cloud Foundry migration phases:

  • Plan: List out all iFlows, Integration packages, certificates, security material, and Connectivity.
  • Prepare: Provision CF subaccount, spaces, Integration Suite, roles, and quotas.
  • Identify Cloud Connector mappings, Neo URLs, destinations, and environment-specific parameters.
  • Notify all sender/receiver system owners about endpoint changes.
  • Migrate: Use SAP-supported tools to migrate packages, iFlows, and mappings.
  • Recreate security material, destinations, and Cloud Connector configurations in CF.
  • Validate: Smoke-test migrated iFlows in lower environments.
  • Update endpoints, monitoring, alerts, and remove hard-coded Neo references.
  • Cutover: Migrate production interfaces, monitor stability, and decommission Neo.

4.Pre-Packaged Integration Content for Sales cloud & Service Cloud V2

One of the real advantages of SAP Integration suite is that SAP ships standard, maintained integration packages on the SAP Business Accelerator Hub (api.sap.com) for the most common S/4HANA and ERP scenarios reducing the amount of integration you need to hand-build.

Key Integration packages in Business Accelerator Hub

  • SAP Sales Cloud V2 with S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition
    Business Partner, Product, Pricing; Quote/Sales Order replication to S/4HANA; Order status feedback to Sales Cloud V2.
  • SAP Service Cloud V2 with S/4HANA (Private Cloud and On-Premise)
    Business Partner (bi-directional), Contacts, Product (S/4HANA as leading), Equipment → Registered Product, Sales Org/.
  • SAP Service Cloud V2 with ERP
    Master Data-Customer (bi-directional), Material (ECC as leading), Sales Org and Transactional data.
  • SAP Service Cloud V2 with SAP Customer Data platform
    Customer and Interactions (activities)
  • SAP Service Cloud V2 for Utilities 
    Utilities specific objects -Master Data, Premise, Contract account.
  • SAP Service Cloud V2 with SAP CPQ
    Product configuration, pricing and quote
  • SAP Service Cloud V2 with SAP Master Data Integration
    Business partner and Product to Service Cloud V2.
  • SAP Service Cloud V2 with SuccessFactors Employee Central
    Employee to Service Cloud V2.
  • Locate the package in the Business Accelerator Hub and review its documentation, prerequisites, supported objects, and limitations.
  • Import the package into your Integration Suite (CF) tenant's Design workspace.
  • Configure environment-specific parameters: endpoints, field mappings, and filter conditions.
  • Create/assign the required security material (V2 / S/4HANA certificate-based/basic authentication as applicable to the scenario).
  • Deploy to a non-production environment and validate against a representative data set.
  • Transport through Dev → Test → Prod.

Configure and Deploy the Required SSC V2 iFlows

Once the standard packages are identified and custom interfaces are mapped, deployment follows a repeatable per-process pattern.

Per-process deployment pattern:

Step 1 — Authentication and connectivity setup

Establish the V2 communication arrangement, communication system, and authentication mechanism required by the specific API and integration scenario. OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials is commonly used, but the exact token endpoint, credentials, and authorisation scopes should be taken from the V2 tenant and API documentation for the specific scenario — not assumed as universal.

  • Create the OAuth2 Client Credentials security material in Cloud Integration before touching the iFlow configuration.
  • Configure BTP Destinations for V2 tenant base URLs; avoid hardcoding environment-specific values in iFlow logic.
  • Validate Cloud Connector if on-premise receivers (e.g., ERP/ECC) are involved.

Step 2 — Configure adapters and deploy

  • Configure sender/receiver adapters with the V2 tenant host, resource paths, and OAuth credential alias.
  • Implement exponential backoff, DLQ routing, and exception sub-processes for downstream failures.
  • Capture correlation IDs from V2 API responses for end-to-end tracing.
  • Deploy to Dev first; validate E2E; promote via TMS.

 5.Adapt Custom iFlows to Point to the V2 REST API

Custom-built V1 iFlows generally require functional and technical redesign, not just an endpoint change. V2 introduces a new API and business-object model, with REST APIs and OData V4 APIs where supported. Therefore, each interface should first be mapped to the appropriate V2 business object, API, and communication scenario.

Adaptation checklist by custom iFlow

  • Assess the interface – Decide whether to adopt, adapt, redesign, or retire the iFlow. Check for equivalent standard Business Accelerator Hub content.
  • Map the business object/API – Identify the V2 business object and API; validate semantics, relationships, partner functions, and code lists.
  • Update the receiver – Replace the V1 service/endpoint with the appropriate V2 API and resource path.
  • Update authentication – Implement the authentication mechanism supported by the V2 communication scenario and maintain the required credentials/security material in Cloud Integration.
  • Rebuild mappings – Rework JSON/XML mappings against V2 payload structures rather than modifying existing V1 mappings.
  • Refactor query logic – Reassess filters, pagination, sorting, and query syntax; do not copy V1 queries without validation.
  • Redesign error handling – Adapt exception handling to V2 HTTP status codes and error-response structures.
  • Reassess retries/idempotency – Validate retry, duplicate-message handling, and sequencing, particularly for event-driven integrations.
  • Review monitoring and performance – Reassess logging, pagination, batch handling, timeouts, and API limits.
  • Test end-to-end – Validate functional scenarios, positive/negative cases, security, error handling, retries, and integration with downstream systems.

The objective is not to replace the V1 endpoint with a V2 endpoint, but to redesign each integration around the V2 business object, API, security model, and integration pattern. SAP's transition guidance also recommends assessing integrations as part of the overall V1-to-V2 transition.

6.Data Migration vs. Integration Cutover — Keep These Separate

Data migration and integration cutovers are related but distinct workstreams and should be planned, owned, and tracked separately.

Workstream

What it covers

Key watch-out

Data Migration

 

DTT, initial load, and delta transfer of supported master and transactional data, including notes, attachments, and extension fields where supported.

DTT scope and restrictions are object-specific. Validate prerequisites and supported data before finalizing the migration scope.

Integration Cutover

Handled by stopping V1 interfaces, completing delta synchronisation, enabling V2 interfaces, and executing reconciliation.

Sequence matters: freeze V1 → complete delta → validate → enable V2 → smoke test → business sign-off → monitor.

 Resource links 

  • SAP Sales Cloud Version 2 – Main Help Portal – overall product documentation, setup, solution guides, integration, APIs, and feature scope. SAP Sales Cloud Version 2 Help Portal
  • V1 → V2 Transition Tools – Readiness Check, Data Transfer Tool, and transition guidance. SAP C4C Transition Tools
  • Communication Systems – useful for communication arrangements, authentication, and external system connectivity. SAP Sales Cloud V2 – Communication Systems
  • V2 APIs – REST APIs and API documentation available through SAP Business Accelerator Hub. SAP Sales Cloud V2 APIs
  • S/4HANA Integration – documentation for integrating Sales Cloud V2 with SAP S/4HANA. SAP Sales Cloud V2 – S/4HANA Integration
  • Outbound Events – useful when evaluating event-based integration instead of traditional synchronous interfaces. SAP Sales Cloud V2 – Outbound Events
  • Transfer your integration scenarios in the Cloud Integration tenant from the Neo environment to SAP Integration Suite- Migrating-cloud-integration-from-neo-environment-to-multi-cloud-foundation

Summary:

Transitioning integrations from SAP Sales & Service Cloud V1 to V2 is not an endpoint migration exercise. It is a combination of:

  • Landscape rationalisation – retire obsolete integrations instead of migrating them.
  • Business object & API mapping – validate business semantics before field mapping.
  • Architecture redesign – adopt REST, events, standard content, or custom solutions as appropriate.
  • Security modernisation – update OAuth, communication arrangements, and certificates.
  • Standard content adoption – use Business Accelerator Hub content wherever applicable.
  • Custom integration redevelopment – redesign rather than simply replace endpoints.
  • Data migration coordination – coordinate data migration separately with integration cutover.

The programme should begin with a complete V1 integration inventory, followed by a decision for each interface: adopt, adapt, redesign, or retire. The Neo-to-CF migration should run as a parallel technical workstream with coordinated testing and cutover.

entry.title: From SEO to MEO: Designing Joule-Ready API Layers for SAP Commerce Cloud
entry.content:
For many years, digital commerce teams have optimized storefronts for two principal consumers: shoppers and search engines. The shopper receives visual navigation, product pages, carts, and checkout journeys. The search engine receives crawlable content, metadata, canonical URLs, structured information, and other discoverability signals.

A third consumer is now becoming architecturally relevant: the machine acting on behalf of a user.

An AI assistant does not necessarily begin with a product listing page or navigate a storefront in the same sequence as a human shopper. It may receive an intent such as:

  • Find products that match these business requirements.
  • Explain whether a product can be ordered for a particular account.
  • Create a draft cart containing approved items.
  • Retrieve the current status of an order.
  • Identify the next valid step in a checkout process.

These requests cannot be handled reliably by optimizing page content alone. They require stable operations, explicit semantics, typed inputs and outputs, authorization rules, confirmation boundaries, and traceable execution.

This article calls that architectural direction Machine Experience Optimization, or MEO.

Important terminology note: MEO is used in this article as a proposed architectural concept. It is not presented as an official SAP product, feature, methodology, or established SAP term.

Table of Contents:

  • 1. What Changes When the Consumer Is a Machine?
  • 2. The Existing SAP Commerce Cloud Foundation
  • 3. What “Joule-Ready” Means in This Architecture
  • 4. Reference Architecture
  • 4.1 Responsibilities of the Intent Facade
  • 5. Start with Intent, Not with Existing Endpoint Names
  • 6. Designing the Machine-Readable Contract
  • 6.1 Example OpenAPI Contract
  • 6.2 Why Use POST for a Search Intent?
  • 6.3 Keep the Output Small and Purpose-Built
  • 7. Illustrative SAP Commerce Cloud Implementation
  • 8. Calling Existing OCC APIs from a Separate Facade
  • 9. Read Operations and Consequential Actions Must Be Separated
  • 9.1 Example Confirmation Contract
  • 9.2 Idempotency
  • 10. Authentication and Authorization
  • 11. Errors Should Be Useful but Non-Sensitive
  • 12. Observability for Machine-Initiated Commerce
  • 13. The Role of Composable Storefront
  • 14. Recommended Proof of Concept
  • Phase 1: Read-Only Intents
  • Phase 2: Draft Intents
  • Phase 3: Consequential Intents
  • 15. Delivery Checklist
  • Discovery
  • Contract Design
  • Implementation
  • Validation
  • 16. What MEO Is Not
  • Conclusion
  • References

 

1. What Changes When the Consumer Is a Machine?

Search engine optimization primarily answers the question, “Can a search engine discover and understand this page?”

Machine Experience Optimization asks a different set of questions:

  • Can an approved machine client identify the correct business operation?
  • Does the operation have an unambiguous purpose?
  • Are its inputs and outputs explicit and machine-readable?
  • Can it distinguish a read request from a consequential business action?
  • Can authorization be evaluated using the user, client, account, base site, and business context?
  • Can retries occur without creating duplicate carts, orders, or other unintended effects?
  • Can the complete request be correlated and audited without exposing sensitive data?

This is not a replacement for SEO. Human storefront experience, accessibility, performance, structured content, and conventional search discoverability remain important. MEO adds another contract: a controlled contract between business intent and executable commerce capabilities.

 

2. The Existing SAP Commerce Cloud Foundation

SAP Commerce Cloud, composable storefront already creates an important architectural separation between the user interface and the commerce platform. SAP describes composable storefront as an Angular-based JavaScript storefront that communicates with SAP Commerce Cloud through the Commerce REST API

The storefront therefore does not need to be the only consumer of every commerce capability. The same underlying commerce services can support additional approved channels, provided that each channel applies appropriate contracts, security, and governance.

OCC, or Omni Commerce Connect, exposes commerce and data services through REST interfaces. Its implementation connects web-service controllers to commerce facades and maps commerce data objects to web-service DTOs. OCC also provides supporting capabilities such as authentication, exception handling, request processing, and selected caching mechanisms.

This produces a useful starting point:

  1. SAP Commerce Cloud contains the commerce models, services, facades, validation, and business rules.
  2. OCC exposes approved platform capabilities through REST APIs.
  3. Composable storefront consumes those APIs for the human-facing experience.
  4. An additional intent-oriented facade can expose carefully selected capabilities to machine consumers.

The intent facade is not intended to duplicate SAP Commerce Cloud. Its purpose is to present a smaller and more stable set of business-oriented operations to consumers that should not need to understand storefront components, page composition, or a large sequence of low-level API calls.

 

3. What “Joule-Ready” Means in This Architecture

In this article, Joule-ready means that an API is deliberately designed so it can be evaluated for controlled use by a Joule capability. It does not mean that every OCC endpoint is automatically available to Joule, or that an out-of-the-box Joule-to-Commerce connector is assumed

SAP documentation distinguishes between Joule skills and Joule agents:

  • A Joule skill is suitable for a predefined and deterministic operation with known inputs and outputs.
  • A Joule agent can select and use tools for more adaptive, multi-step problem solving.

Both models benefit from well-defined APIs. A skill may invoke one deterministic operation. An agent may use multiple tools, but each tool still needs an accurate description, constrained inputs, predictable outputs, and explicit authorization.

A Joule-ready commerce API should therefore have:

  • A business-oriented operation name.
  • A concise and accurate operation description.
  • A structured input schema.
  • A bounded output schema.
  • Clear read-versus-write semantics.
  • Documented authorization requirements.
  • Known validation and error outcomes.
  • Confirmation rules for consequential actions.
  • Idempotency behavior for retried write operations.
  • Correlation and audit information.

 

4. Reference Architecture

A practical design places a governed intent facade between machine consumers and SAP Commerce Cloud APIs.

Human Channel

Human Channel

 Machine Channel

Machine Channel

The storefront and the machine channel can share the intent facade when that is useful, or the storefront can continue using OCC connectors directly while the machine channel uses the facade. The correct choice depends on the existing solution, performance model, ownership boundaries, and release strategy.

The central design principle is:

Do not require an AI client to reconstruct a business task from rendered HTML, storefront component state, or a long chain of low-level endpoints. Expose a small, explicit, governed business operation.

4.1 Responsibilities of the Intent Facade

The facade can perform responsibilities that should not be delegated to a language model:

  • Validate mandatory inputs.
  • Resolve the applicable base site, language, and currency.
  • Propagate an authorized user or technical-client context.
  • Apply account and organizational boundaries.
  • Call approved OCC endpoints or application services.
  • Aggregate multiple technical responses into one business response.
  • Remove data that is unnecessary for the requested purpose.
  • Normalize errors into a documented schema.
  • Apply idempotency and retry protection.
  • Emit correlation and audit records.

The facade should not silently bypass Commerce authorization, pricing, product eligibility, stock, customer-account, checkout, or order validation rules. SAP Commerce Cloud remains the system responsible for its commerce business behavior.

 

5. Start with Intent, Not with Existing Endpoint Names

A common mistake is to expose every existing API operation to an assistant and expect the model to work out the correct sequence. This increases ambiguity, token usage, coupling, and the probability of an invalid action.

Instead, begin with a limited intent inventory.

IntentOperation TypePossible ContractConfirmation
Find productsReadfindOrderableProductsNot normally required
Explain product eligibilityReadgetProductEligibilityNot normally required
Check order statusReadgetOrderStatusNot normally required
Create a draft cartWritecreateDraftCartDepends on business policy
Add or change a cart itemWriteupdateDraftCartRecommended before execution or finalization
Place an orderConsequential writeplaceOrderExplicit confirmation required

Note: The operation names in this article are illustrative custom names. They are not presented as standard SAP OCC endpoints.

 

6. Designing the Machine-Readable Contract

The quality of the API description matters because names and descriptions become part of how people, integration tooling, and AI capabilities interpret the operation.

6.1 Example OpenAPI Contract

The following is an illustrative custom API contract. It sits above existing SAP Commerce Cloud services and is not an out-of-the-box SAP API specification.

openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: Commerce Intent API
  version: 1.0.0
  description: >
    Governed business operations for approved machine and
    conversational commerce consumers.

paths:
  /api/v1/intents/products:search:
    post:
      operationId: findOrderableProducts
      summary: Find products that can be evaluated for ordering
      description: >
        Searches for products using an explicit base site, language,
        currency, and authorized user context. The operation is
        read-only and does not create or modify a cart.
      security:
        - oauth2: [commerce.products.read]
      parameters:
        - in: header
          name: X-Correlation-ID
          required: true
          schema:
            type: string
            maxLength: 100
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/ProductIntentRequest'
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Matching products
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/ProductIntentResponse'
        '400':
          description: Invalid request
        '401':
          description: Authentication required
        '403':
          description: The principal is not authorized
        '429':
          description: Request limit exceeded

components:
  securitySchemes:
    oauth2:
      type: oauth2
      flows:
        clientCredentials:
          tokenUrl: https://authorization.example.invalid/oauth/token
          scopes:
            commerce.products.read: Read product information

  schemas:
    ProductIntentRequest:
      type: object
      additionalProperties: false
      required:
        - query
        - baseSite
        - language
        - currency
      properties:
        query:
          type: string
          minLength: 2
          maxLength: 200
        baseSite:
          type: string
          maxLength: 40
        language:
          type: string
          pattern: '^[a-z]{2}(-[A-Z]{2})?$'
        currency:
          type: string
          pattern: '^[A-Z]{3}$'
        accountId:
          type: string
          maxLength: 80
        page:
          type: integer
          minimum: 0
          default: 0
        pageSize:
          type: integer
          minimum: 1
          maximum: 50
          default: 10

    ProductIntentResponse:
      type: object
      required:
        - products
        - pagination
        - correlationId
      properties:
        products:
          type: array
          items:
            $ref: '#/components/schemas/IntentProduct'
        pagination:
          $ref: '#/components/schemas/Pagination'
        correlationId:
          type: string

    IntentProduct:
      type: object
      required:
        - code
        - name
        - productUrl
      properties:
        code:
          type: string
        name:
          type: string
        productUrl:
          type: string
          format: uri
        formattedPrice:
          type: string
        stockStatus:
          type: string
        eligibilityStatus:
          type: string
          enum:
            - ELIGIBLE
            - NOT_ELIGIBLE
            - REQUIRES_CONTEXT
            - UNKNOWN

    Pagination:
      type: object
      properties:
        page:
          type: integer
        pageSize:
          type: integer
        totalPages:
          type: integer

6.2 Why Use POST for a Search Intent?

A conventional product-search API frequently uses an HTTP GET request. A custom intent facade may use POST when the query has a structured request body, when complex filters would otherwise produce an excessively long URL, or when logging query parameters in infrastructure must be avoided.

This should be an explicit API design decision. It does not change the operation into a business write. The OpenAPI description should clearly state that the operation is read-only and has no commerce side effect.

6.3 Keep the Output Small and Purpose-Built

Returning every property available in a product DTO is rarely necessary. A machine-oriented response should contain only the information required for the approved scenario.

For product discovery, that may include:

  • Canonical product code.
  • Display name.
  • Canonical storefront URL.
  • Localized price representation, where authorized and applicable.
  • Stock or availability status at the appropriate level.
  • An explicit eligibility status.
  • A reason code that is safe to expose.

The response should avoid internal model details, unrestricted customer data, implementation-specific database identifiers, secrets, or fields that the caller does not need.

 

7. Illustrative SAP Commerce Cloud Implementation

One implementation approach is to create a custom OCC extension or a separate backend-for-frontend service. The choice should be made according to the existing architecture, extension strategy, operational ownership, latency requirements, and upgrade policy.

The following Java example illustrates the separation between a controller, an intent service, and the underlying Commerce integration. Package names and DTOs are illustrative.

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/intents")
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class CommerceIntentController {

    private final CommerceIntentService commerceIntentService;

    @PostMapping(
        value = "/products:search",
        consumes = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE,
        produces = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE
    )
    @PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('commerce.products.read')")
    public ResponseEntity<ProductIntentResponse> findOrderableProducts(
            @RequestHeader("X-Correlation-ID") String correlationId,
            @Valid @RequestBody ProductIntentRequest request,
            Authentication authentication) {

        IntentPrincipal principal =
            IntentPrincipal.from(authentication);

        ProductIntentResponse response =
            commerceIntentService.findOrderableProducts(
                request,
                principal,
                correlationId
            );

        return ResponseEntity.ok(response);
    }
}

The controller should not contain product-selection or account-eligibility logic. That belongs in domain services, Commerce facades, or existing application services.

@service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class DefaultCommerceIntentService
        implements CommerceIntentService {

    private final ProductSearchFacade productSearchFacade;
    private final ProductEligibilityService eligibilityService;
    private final IntentProductMapper intentProductMapper;
    private final IntentAuthorizationService authorizationService;

    @Override
    public ProductIntentResponse findOrderableProducts(
            ProductIntentRequest request,
            IntentPrincipal principal,
            String correlationId) {

        authorizationService.assertProductReadAllowed(
            principal,
            request.baseSite(),
            request.accountId()
        );

        ProductSearchCriteria criteria =
            ProductSearchCriteria.builder()
                .query(request.query())
                .baseSite(request.baseSite())
                .language(request.language())
                .currency(request.currency())
                .page(request.page())
                .pageSize(request.pageSize())
                .build();

        ProductSearchResult searchResult =
            productSearchFacade.search(criteria);

        List<IntentProduct> products =
            searchResult.products().stream()
                .map(product -> {
                    ProductEligibility eligibility =
                        eligibilityService.evaluate(
                            product.code(),
                            request.accountId(),
                            principal
                        );

                    return intentProductMapper.map(
                        product,
                        eligibility
                    );
                })
                .toList();

        return ProductIntentResponse.builder()
            .products(products)
            .pagination(
                Pagination.from(searchResult.pagination())
            )
            .correlationId(correlationId)
            .build();
    }
}

This example demonstrates several important boundaries:

  • The authenticated principal is passed into authorization.
  • Base-site and account context are explicit.
  • The response is mapped to a dedicated machine contract.
  • The machine contract does not expose the complete internal product model.
  • A correlation identifier is returned to support diagnostics.

 

8. Calling Existing OCC APIs from a Separate Facade

When the intent layer is implemented outside the SAP Commerce Cloud runtime, it can invoke approved OCC operations. The exact URL, authentication flow, fields, DTOs, and endpoint availability must be validated against the SAP Commerce Cloud release and the project configuration.

export interface CommerceProductClient {
  searchProducts(
    context: CommerceContext,
    query: ProductSearchQuery,
    accessToken: string,
    correlationId: string
  ): Promise<OccProductSearchResponse>;
}

export class OccCommerceProductClient
  implements CommerceProductClient {

  constructor(
    private readonly httpClient: HttpClient,
    private readonly configuration: CommerceConfiguration
  ) {}

  async searchProducts(
    context: CommerceContext,
    query: ProductSearchQuery,
    accessToken: string,
    correlationId: string
  ): Promise<OccProductSearchResponse> {

    const baseUrl = this.configuration.getOccBaseUrl(
      context.baseSite
    );

    const response = await this.httpClient.get(
      `${baseUrl}/products/search`,
      {
        headers: {
          Authorization: `Bearer ${accessToken}`,
          "X-Correlation-ID": correlationId,
          Accept: "application/json"
        },
        params: {
          query: query.text,
          currentPage: query.page,
          pageSize: query.pageSize,
          lang: context.language,
          curr: context.currency
        },
        timeout: 5000
      }
    );

    return response.data as OccProductSearchResponse;
  }
}

The intent service should map the retrieved OCC response into its own versioned response contract. Passing the complete OCC payload directly to a machine client would couple that client to the current OCC DTO and could expose fields outside the intended business purpose.

 

9. Read Operations and Consequential Actions Must Be Separated

Product discovery is fundamentally different from order placement. It is useful to classify operations using at least three categories:

  1. Read operations: Retrieve products, eligibility, cart state, or order status.
  2. Reversible or draft operations: Create a draft cart or modify unsubmitted cart entries.
  3. Consequential operations: Place an order, commit payment-related choices, submit a return, or make another business commitment.

A consequential operation should not be executed merely because the initial natural-language request appears to imply consent. The design should create a confirmation boundary.

 

9.1 Example Confirmation Contract

{
  "action": "PLACE_ORDER",
  "status": "CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED",
  "confirmationId": "conf-81f86a",
  "expiresAt": "2026-09-04T18:30:00Z",
  "summary": {
    "cartId": "00018492",
    "itemCount": 3,
    "currency": "USD",
    "total": "1250.00",
    "deliveryAddressId": "address-17"
  },
  "allowedResponses": [
    "CONFIRM",
    "CANCEL"
  ]
}

The confirmation identifier should be short-lived, bound to the authorized user and exact transaction state, and invalidated if the underlying cart changes.

9.2 Idempotency

A retried operation must not unintentionally create duplicate business transactions. A write operation can require an idempotency key:

POST /api/v1/intents/carts
Authorization: Bearer <access-token>
Idempotency-Key: 22a8f87e-4fff-4ec5-87cb-2667cd77144d
X-Correlation-ID: 616aebaf-6887-4cd7-93ba-8fe4e72cc263
Content-Type: application/json

The service should define how long the key remains valid, which authenticated principal owns it, and what response is returned when the same key is received with a different payload.

Note: The keys above are randomized and are not actual in any way.

 

10. Authentication and Authorization

SAP Commerce Cloud OCC uses OAuth-based mechanisms for authentication and authorization. The authorization design for the intent layer should nevertheless be evaluated independently because the machine client, end-user identity, and business account may represent different security contexts.

The design should answer the following questions explicitly:

  • Is the client operating as itself or on behalf of a user?
  • Which operations can a technical client invoke?
  • Which scopes or authorities are required?
  • How is an end-user identity propagated or exchanged?
  • How are base-site and customer-account boundaries enforced?
  • Can a client request information for a different account by changing an input field?
  • Where are authorization decisions recorded?
  • How are tokens, secrets, and refresh credentials protected?

Authorization should be checked at more than the URL level. A principal may have permission to call a product API but still be restricted from viewing account-specific prices, ordering a regulated product, using a particular ship-to address, or accessing another user’s order.

 

11. Errors Should Be Useful but Non-Sensitive

Machine consumers require structured errors. Unstructured stack traces or HTML error pages are unsuitable and may expose internal implementation details.

{
  "error": {
    "code": "ACCOUNT_CONTEXT_REQUIRED",
    "message": "An authorized account context is required.",
    "retryable": false,
    "correlationId": "616aebaf-6887-4cd7-93ba-8fe4e72cc263"
  }
}

Use stable error codes and safe messages. Log the detailed technical cause in the appropriate secured operational system, linked through the correlation identifier. Do not place access tokens, payment information, passwords, or unnecessary personal data in API logs.

 

12. Observability for Machine-Initiated Commerce

Traditional storefront analytics answer questions about page views, sessions, clicks, and conversions. An intent layer needs an additional operational view.

Useful technical measures include:

  • Requests by operation identifier.
  • Successful, rejected, and failed requests.
  • Authorization-denial categories.
  • Validation-error categories.
  • Latency of the facade and downstream Commerce calls.
  • Rate-limit and quota events.
  • Confirmation issued, accepted, rejected, or expired.
  • Idempotent replay events.
  • Downstream OCC error categories.

These measures should be designed with privacy and security requirements. A useful operational record normally needs the operation name, outcome, timing, principal classification, tenant or site context, and correlation identifier. It may not need the user’s original natural-language prompt.

 

13. The Role of Composable Storefront

Very importantly:

Spoiler
MEO does not remove the storefront.

Composable storefront remains the visual environment for product discovery, comparison, account management, cart review, checkout, and other customer journeys. In fact, a machine response should frequently return canonical storefront links so that a user can continue in the governed visual experience.

For example, a product-search response may return:

{
  "code": "PRODUCT-10031",
  "name": "Example Product",
  "productUrl": "https://store.example.invalid/p/PRODUCT-10031",
  "eligibilityStatus": "ELIGIBLE",
  "nextActions": [
    {
      "type": "OPEN_STOREFRONT",
      "label": "View product"
    },
    {
      "type": "CREATE_DRAFT_CART",
      "label": "Add to a draft cart"
    }
  ]
}

The human and machine experiences should therefore complement each other:

  • The machine channel reduces the work required to identify the correct capability.
  • The storefront provides rich visual review and established user interaction.
  • The Commerce platform continues to apply business rules and transaction processing.

 

14. Recommended Proof of Concept

A controlled proof of concept should start with a small number of operations rather than an end-to-end autonomous checkout.

Phase 1: Read-Only Intents

  • Find orderable products.
  • Retrieve product details.
  • Check order status for the authenticated user.

Phase 2: Draft Intents

  • Create a draft cart.
  • Add an item to a draft cart.
  • Return a storefront link for cart review.

Phase 3: Consequential Intents

  • Validate checkout readiness.
  • Generate a transaction summary.
  • Require explicit confirmation.
  • Submit the transaction using idempotency protection.

Each phase should include contract testing, authorization testing, negative testing, rate-limit testing, logging review, and an assessment of the data made available to the consuming AI capability.

 

15. Delivery Checklist

Discovery

  • Inventory the existing OCC APIs and custom Commerce services.
  • Identify the smallest valuable set of business intents.
  • Classify data according to applicable organizational requirements.
  • Confirm Joule, Joule Studio, and related service availability and licensing for the landscape.

Contract Design

  • Use business verbs and precise operation descriptions.
  • Define mandatory context such as base site, language, currency, account, and user.
  • Separate read operations from write operations.
  • Define pagination, errors, confirmation, retry, and idempotency behavior.
  • Version the machine contract independently of the storefront UI.

Implementation

  • Reuse supported OCC operations before creating custom APIs.
  • Keep controllers thin and business rules in the appropriate service layer.
  • Map platform DTOs to minimized intent DTOs.
  • Apply OAuth, roles, contextual authorization, and rate controls.
  • Add end-to-end correlation identifiers.

Validation

  • Test valid and invalid schemas.
  • Test cross-account and cross-site access attempts.
  • Test repeated write requests.
  • Test modified transactions after confirmation is issued.
  • Review logs for sensitive information.
  • Validate behavior against the exact SAP Commerce Cloud release in use.

 

16. What MEO Is Not

MEO should not be used as a justification for:

  • Making all OCC APIs publicly accessible.
  • Letting an AI model bypass Commerce authorization.
  • Sending complete customer, product, cart, or order objects to a model without a defined purpose.
  • Executing an order based only on an inferred user intention.
  • Placing business rules inside prompts instead of governed application services.
  • Coupling machine operations to visual page markup.
  • Claiming an SAP-supported integration without validating the applicable SAP documentation, release, entitlement, and product scope.

 

Conclusion

Composable architecture is commonly discussed in terms of replaceable user-interface components and API-first commerce. The rise of AI assistants introduces a further requirement: business capabilities must be understandable to machines without becoming uncontrolled.

SAP Commerce Cloud already provides a strong separation between composable storefront and the Commerce platform through REST APIs. The next architectural step is not to expose every low-level API to an assistant. It is to create a small, semantic, governed layer that translates approved intent into authorized Commerce operations

That is the purpose of Machine Experience Optimization:

  • SEO makes content discoverable.
  • Composable storefront makes the experience modular.
  • OCC makes commerce capabilities accessible through APIs.
  • MEO makes selected business intent explicit, bounded, and governable for machine consumers.

The most successful implementation will not be the one that gives an AI system the widest access. It will be the one that provides the clearest contract, the smallest necessary data set, the strongest authorization, and the safest path from user intent to commerce outcome.

References

  • SAP Help Portal: About Composable Storefront
  • SAP Help Portal: Composable Storefront API
  • SAP Help Portal: Omni Commerce Connect
  • SAP Help Portal: OCC API Implementation
  • SAP Help Portal: OAuth 2.0 for OCC
  • SAP Help Portal: Create AI Capabilities with Joule Studio
  • SAP Help Portal: What Is Joule Studio, Classic Edition?

Note: All custom endpoints, DTOs, scopes, source-code packages, domain names, product identifiers, and transaction values in this article are illustrative. Validate the applicable APIs, versions, security configuration, licensing, and supported integration approach for your own SAP landscape.

entry.title: Get your hands on the new MCP Gateway capability in SAP Integration Suite
entry.content:
Many of you have probably already noticed that the SAP Developer Center recently received a great new updated look and feel. I have always been a big fan of this resource for getting the latest technical updates, enablement and, first and foremost, the hands-on tutorials.

So I wanted to use this opportunity to write my very first tutorial myself – and what better topic to pick than the new MCP Gateway capability in SAP Integration Suite?

If you haven't come across it yet: Think of the MCP Gateway as the enterprise control plane for MCP. An MCP server hosts the tools, but the Gateway decides who gets to use them and how. It takes care of authentication, authorization, rate limiting and payload protection, and gives you full monitoring and traceability on top. The best part is that it brings tools from SAP APIs, non-SAP APIs, integration flows, data sources and even external MCP servers together behind one single, governed entry point.

In my hands-on you get to experience this new capability end to end with a real third-party application – from creating a hosted and managed MCP server from scratch all the way to testing it properly with the MCP Inspector.

In detail, you will learn:

  • How to work with the new API artifact in SAP Integration Suite
  • How to host custom MCP servers with the MCP Gateway
  • How to govern your MCP resources by enforcing policies
  • How to make your MCP servers discoverable and consumable in the Developer Hub
  • How to test your results with the MCP Inspector

So get your SAP BTP trial account today and start the tutorial right away: Get started with the MCP Gateway in SAP Integration Suite

Stay tuned!
